speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In those 27 years, society, attitudes towards religion, the environment and more have changed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We reviewed MRHA and we decided to amend it, keep it relevant, keep it effective.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this speech, I will touch on three aspects.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, the background to MRHA, reasons why it was introduced in 1990; second, a brief look at relevant events around the world, the extent of religious harmony and our experience over the past 27 years; and third, set out the rationale for the amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling, will speak on the specific provisions in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The rationale for MRHA was set out in a White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One: religious harmony is a necessary condition for us to survive as a country.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government needed to set out a set of “working rules” on how different religious groups interact with one another.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One such rule was that religious groups should not do anything that causes disharmony, ill-will or hostility among different religious groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A key tenet of many religions is to propagate their faith but, in Singapore, we want it to be done sensitively.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another rule, if I may highlight, is that religious groups should not venture into politics and political parties should not use religion to get popular support.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The White Paper also recognised it would be unwise to assume that all religious groups will recognise the Rules of Prudence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, in our context, in fact in any country, if these rules were ignored, that could seriously damage our social fabric and our political, economic fabric.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The White Paper then said legislation was, therefore, necessary because we wanted to take pre-emptive action to maintain religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It could also consider other matters that affected the maintenance of religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think we all recognise the power of religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has been and is a force for much good.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Major religions have transformed societies in positive ways.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are the bedrock of core societal values: compassion, kindness, generosity.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The collective efforts of a number of different religious organisations and groups, their values and their faith have also helped to make Singapore what it is today.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, we recognise that religion has also been used and can be used by bad actors as a rallying point for violence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Also, by bad actors as a rallying point to pursue political power, often with bad outcomes for societies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 1990, the Government was very aware of the good that religion can bring about, but also how it can be abused by some.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the question was how to keep the good, allow a large measure of freedom and also keep out the bad?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, emphasise the constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion – the right of every person to practise his or her beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the Government, as a matter of policy, made sure that religion remained accessible to all Singaporeans who wish to access it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, land is continuously set aside in our residential estates.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Every time we plan an estate, we take into account religious needs for worship for all religions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government helped to establish the Mosque Building and MENDAKI Fund, which made it easier to mobilise the community and build mosques.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, the Government itself is secular.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not like secularism in some other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The example I spoke about in April this year before this House was France.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There, the state will not intervene in religious matters, even if an act or speech offends other religions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I explained this in some detail in my Parliamentary Statement in April before this House.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government does not privilege any religious group.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we also do not allow any religious group to be attacked or insulted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we actively encourage interfaith dialogues, activities to foster mutual understanding and respect.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, we keep to the position that no religious group should influence Government policy and decision-making.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That was the background for the passing of MRHA in 1990.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the last 27 years since it was passed, there have been some significant changes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That, we can see, is particularly so in this region – look at Indonesia, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Rising religiosity, by itself, can be a force for considerable good, as I explained earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there can be trouble when it is exploited by bad actors, for example, for identity politics.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we look at Europe, far-right movements play up anxieties against Muslims and other minorities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we look nearer in this region, in Myanmar, there is religious conflict between the majority Buddhists and the Rohingya Muslim minority.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Buddhist monks enter the political scene and say they are defending the Buddhist Myanmar against Islamisation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we look at Sri Lanka, some have sought to radicalise Buddhists by claims that all of Sri Lanka should be exclusively Buddhist.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had a 2013 Buddhist attack on a mosque; 2014, anti-Muslim riots which resulted in a 10-day national state of emergency; and last year, more anti-Muslim riots.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Buddhist monks have also disrupted Christian church services.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: India was established in 1947 as a pluralist nation and home that comprises people of many religions, sects and ethnicities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Their constitution provides no particular religion with special status.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A writer points out that the party that champions secularism, the Congress Party, during the 1984 national elections, moved away from being tied to secularism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It won by riding on Hindu majoritarian politics.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: By 2019, to regain power, the Congress Party dropped the word "secularism" from its manifesto.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It tells you how far things have come.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is the party of Nehru and Gandhi.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The writer, Kanchan Chandra, says that through the years, Indian politicians have swayed from one side to another, overly championing minority interests, or giving in too much to the majority's desires.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And over time, this generated feelings of unfairness, from both the minority and majority religionists.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Secularism is an ideal but it is difficult to get it right and get the balance right.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our Constitution guarantees the freedom of religion, but so do the constitutions of many other countries, including the United States (US).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that has not prevented the rise of identity politics.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second trend that I want to touch on is the increasing violence from conflicts that have been fueled by religious hate speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Once hate speech is systemically developed and normalised, it destroys social cohesion, erodes shared values and lays the foundation for violence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I spoke about this quite extensively, to a great extent in this House in April.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Hate speech is also fuel for religious violence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2018, Pew Research Centre did a study that showed that two years earlier in 2016, more than 25% of the countries in the world experienced a high incidence of hostilities involving religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look around, you see many examples and I gave many examples a few months ago.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The third trend that I want to touch on is the Internet and social media.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Internet has been used to mobilise hatred and mob attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has provided for anonymity that allows unfettered expressions and religious intolerance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Internet access has made it easier for people to be influenced by extremist ideologies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And collectively, social media can invoke irrational fear of both the majority and the minority groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Parts of the Internet are already turning into hothouses of hate; like-minded bigots find one another and gather online.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are helped by Internet platforms where algorithms allow hate to go viral.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we look at India, in 2014, photos of venerated Hindu figures were morphed in "derogatory" manner and circulated on social media.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Lots of people took to the streets, asking for the blood of the offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Indonesia, you have preachers, some of whom have vast followings on social media and are influencers with a force of their own.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can mobilise huge crowds and can make part of the Muslim community susceptible to identity politics.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Right next to us, on the other side, you have the "Buy Muslim First" campaign in Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has been gaining momentum, going around on WhatsApp messages.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is now seen as a boycott of goods and services produced by non-Muslims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Government leaders have attempted to intervene but, so far, the impact has been minimal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If this continues to grow, it will stoke Muslim versus non-Muslim sentiments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fourth trend I will touch on is foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members know about it and the Internet makes it much more possible.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, let me now turn to the situation in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have been spared most of this trouble in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the last 60 years, the Government has been even-handed in the treatment of all religions and religious groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We actively protect religious diversity, but also emphasise our common spaces and our shared experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Commitment encourages day-to-day positive interactions so that people can work and live together harmoniously.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Beyond institutional structures, we also have laws in place that seek to ensure that no one exploits fault lines.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because of these policies, the laws and enforcement, we have created some norms and values within Singapore which make us unique and different from many other places.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That could make us particularly susceptible to fault lines deepening, because you are so diverse in such a small place.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The poll deals with ethnicity, not religion, but I think you can draw some conclusions from that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think you take the surveys and studies in context.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Just because people say we are No 1 does not automatically mean we are No 1.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I think we look our lived experiences, lived realities and the findings are consistent with our lived experiences in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have described the developments around the world that we should be concerned about.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is easy for religious movements in other countries to affect us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A new way of thinking, or revolutions like the 1979 Iranian Revolution, swept through the world; the ideas, come through here, too.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to put in some circuit breakers to prevent events relating to religion from affecting us negatively.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Protection is provided to religious groups and their members, as well as non-religious groups and the members of such groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Action can be taken if any religious group or its member attacks another religious group using religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But action can also be taken if a religious group, using religion, attacks a non-religious group, say, for example, they attack a Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer (LGBTQ) group or individuals on the basis of religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But equally, if a religious group or its member is attacked by any non-religious group or person, say, again, LGBTQ, then action can also be taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, we need to put in place measures to safeguard against foreign actors who attempt to use religion to divide our local communities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also introduces local leadership requirements for religious organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will not apply these requirements to spiritual leaders and preachers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many of them come from overseas and it is not our intent to constrain the practice of religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, the MRHA allows the Government to issue a Restraining Order (RO) to anyone who threatens religious harmony – that has been there all along.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Currently, it requires a 14-day notice period to be given.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will introduce the Community Remedial Initiative (CRI).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a new tool that focuses on restoration and rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some Members may recall an incident a few days ago where the Young Sikh Association reached out to a social media influencer, Ms Sheena Phua.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She had uploaded a picture showing two Sikh men in white turbans at the recent Formula One Grand Prix and referred to them as “huge obstructions”.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She was accused of being racist and slighting Sikhism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It would have been entirely understandable for the Sikh community to criticise her, but the Young Sikh Association took a different path and, in many ways, a very commendable path.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They reached out and invited her to visit the gurdwara so that they could educate her about Sikhism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These young men understood that, at times, insensitive and derogatory comments can come from a place of ignorance and that the better and more sustainable path is not of hate or taking sides, but of friendship, respect and learning about one another.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Malminderjit Singh, the secretary of the Sikh Advisory Board, called the actions of these young men and, I quote, a "First-world response to a third-world incident".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This incident, in fact, encapsulates the spirit of the CRI.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will not be compulsory because we do not want to force a person of one religion to compulsorily, say, step into another place of religious worship if there are religious reasons why that person may not wish to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not want to compel them to do some things that they may not wish to do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will leave it as a matter of their own conscience and what they are prepared to do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But that will be taken into account when deciding on the actions that are subsequently taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The philosophy is that it is much better if people reach out to one another and get a better understanding of one another's religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, these are the changes and they are being proposed after a lot of thought, consultations and, as Members will know, with considerable support from the different religious communities from all the major faiths.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have come out after they saw the Bill and after it was introduced in Parliament to give their support.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I hope that Members will likewise support it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Minister for Home Affairs has set out the broad rationale on the need for the MRHA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: He also explained why we need to amend the MRHA to ensure that it remains effective.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will now set out the Government’s position and provide details on the key amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, safeguards against foreign influence that affect religious harmony.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Minister for Home Affairs has presented examples worldwide that show how foreign influence have impacted religious harmony in those communities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will take active steps to prevent foreign influence from affecting our religious harmony.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many of our religious organisations take guidance on key tenets of their faith from their counterparts or superiors who are overseas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our religious groups serve both Singaporeans and non-Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, it is not possible to say that we cannot have foreign influence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we must safeguard against malicious foreign influence which seeks to undermine religious harmony here.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In Sri Lanka, as a result of the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, investigations uncovered a link between extremism and funding and donations from the Middle East.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The founder of the Centre for Islamic Guidance in Sri Lanka, Mohamed Aliyar, was arrested on charges related to the financing of terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Centre for Islamic Guidance was partly funded by countries in the Middle East and he was closely linked to Zahran Hashim, a radical preacher who allegedly mentored many of the Easter attack bombers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In looking at the safeguards against foreign influence, they are structured so that there will be baseline requirements which all religious groups will be subject to.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If there are specific threats, the Government can take more targeted action.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The disclosure threshold of S$10,000 was set after discussions with the major apex religious organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We wanted to balance the objective of preventing foreign influence and not make it too onerous at the same time for religious organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are not saying that any donation below S$10,000 is not a concern.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Or that any donation above S$10,000 is malicious.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government will make assessments to determine if there is malicious foreign influence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To reduce the administrative burden on religious groups, we have provided for exemptions to this requirement in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, anonymous cash donations received through donation boxes at religious institutions or received during a collection during worship rites or services are exempted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Donations received from Permanent Residents (PRs) as well as foreigners who are on long-term passes issued by the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) or the Ministry of Manpower do not need to be disclosed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If a religious group is incorporated as a company, the requirements will apply on the positions analogous to President, Secretary or Treasurer, for example, the Chairman, Managing Director and Directors of the company.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If the religious group was set up as a partnership, the equivalent position would be the Partners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 13 inserts the new sections 16D and 16E which give effect to this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The leadership requirements do not apply to spiritual leaders, unless they hold such executive positions in the religious group.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We recognise that there are some religious groups which would not be able to meet these requirements, such as those who serve primarily foreigners who live and work in Singapore, or which are set up as single entities operating across different countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have been engaging some of these groups and are prepared to consider exemptions from these new leadership requirements for them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will be granted on a case-by-case basis, as long as there are no security concerns.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Religious groups will be required to declare any foreign affiliations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The safeguard for foreign affiliations is for disclosure purposes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have sought to set the baseline requirements at a level that minimises regulatory burden on the religious groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If, however, we have indications that there is a risk of foreign influence that can affect religious harmony, the proposed Bill will allow us to take more targeted actions in the areas of foreign donations and leadership.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 5 specifically expands the current scope of the RO under section 8 of MRHA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This allows the Government to take targeted action in the areas of donation and leadership of local religious groups where there is indication that there is a risk of foreign influence that can affect religious harmony.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The safeguards for the issuance of the RO against religious groups will be the same as those for the issuance of RO against individuals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: PCRH will hear representations and review the RO after it has been issued.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: PCRH will be able to call any person to provide information to them and PCRH will make a recommendation to the President, who will continue to have the power to confirm, cancel or vary the RO.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The additional safeguards will require religious groups to take on more work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They understand that more work is required but, at the same time, the religious groups acknowledge the importance of such safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Any religious group that needs more time to comply with these requirements can work out appropriate interim arrangements with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will now move on to the updating of the RO that can be issued against individuals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MRHA currently provides that an RO can be issued against: (a) any individual who does or says anything that causes religious disharmony; (b) any religious leader or member of a religious group that mixes religion and politics, and any person inciting a religious leader or religious group to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The RO can prevent this individual from addressing religious groups, or being involved in producing or distributing publications produced by religious groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The scope of the RO was drawn up nearly 30 years ago, before the advent of the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It caters primarily to offline modes of communication.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Social media has enabled offensive posts to go viral in a matter of seconds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is now, thus, a need for the Government to update the RO to take swift action against such posts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This allows us to stem religiously offensive posts at its source quickly, before it spreads.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, the scope of the RO will now include requiring the individual to stop undertaking any "communications activity" relating to the religiously offensive material.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will include the removal of any material that has been posted on the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The safeguards remain unchanged from what they were before.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The individual and the religious group which the individual belongs to can make representations to PCRH.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The RO will be considered by PCRH and ultimately confirmed, canceled or varied by the President.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clauses 2, 5 and 6 give effect to this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To maintain religious harmony, it is not enough to just restrain bad behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When there has been some damage, we need to find a way to soothe communal tensions and repair disrupted ties among the communities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our experience with cases of religious disharmony is that the most effective resolution occurs when the offender displays remorse over his actions and makes amends directly to the offended party.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is frequently facilitated by their religious groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, the offender reflects on his actions and better understands the multi-religious context in which he lives; second, the offended community is given a chance to speak with and accept the apology by the offender.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This goes a long way in soothing communal tensions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is, hence, a need for a new tool in MRHA which focuses on restoration and rehabilitation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 13 introduces the new section 16H which gives effect to this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some examples of remedial actions under the CRI include issuance of a public or private apology, or participating in activities that promote religious harmony.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In determining the appropriate actions, the Minister will consult with the religious leaders, though the final decision rests with him.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The alleged offender can refuse to take up this offer and the non-completion or refusal of CRI, will not be a criminal offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, if the offender agrees to complete the remedial actions and does so, the Minister undertakes not to refer this case for criminal prosecution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: CRI will not be issued to every case where an individual engages in conduct which leads to religious disharmony.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Minister will have to exercise judgement in each case to take the most appropriate course of action.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, if the conduct is very egregious, such as when the offender incites violence, then this case is clearly not suitable for CRI.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Cases of egregious conduct relating to religious disharmony used to be dealt with under the Penal Code, in section 267C and sections 295 to 298A.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will now speak about the porting over of these religion-related offences from the Penal Code to MRHA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We wanted to make MRHA a comprehensive Act which provides for a full range of legislative levers to deal with the maintenance of religious harmony.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the porting over of these offences, we approach it in two ways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: An offence of urging violence against another person or group is more serious than offences of insulting or ridiculing a religion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Religious leaders have a greater ability to influence and mobilise their followers, as compared to lay persons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is the case even when they speak to their followers in private capacities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As such, religious leaders will be subject to a lower threshold for offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 14 inserts the new section 17E, which introduces offences of urging violence on religious grounds against any person or group, and offences of urging violence against religious groups or persons who belong to these groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This sends a strong signal that the weaponisation of religion to urge violence or force to be used against any person is unacceptable in our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is the most serious offence in MRHA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 14 also inserts the new section 17F, which introduces offences of inciting hatred, ill-will or hostility against a religious group, and offences of insulting a religion or wounding the religious feelings of a person.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For offenders who are not religious leaders, an additional element needs to be proven for these offences, that is, that their conduct would threaten the public peace or public order in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For religious leaders, there is no need to prove this element.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The defences for these offences are different for religious leaders and non-religious leaders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It will be a defence for offenders who are not religious leaders to prove that their conduct could reasonably be taken to indicate that the parties desired for it to be heard or seen only by themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In other words, private conduct will not be covered by the offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For religious leaders, in addition to proving that they were engaged in private conduct, there is an additional requirement that the private conduct was a domestic communication.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: An example would be if a religious leader in another country urges his affiliate group in Singapore to rise up and attack another religious group, this will be considered an offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We acknowledge that it may be difficult to enforce these offences extraterritorially.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But this signals our commitment to protect our religious harmony, even when the threats originate from beyond our shores.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: With the porting over of religion-related offences from the Penal Code to MRHA, we will repeal religion-related offences in sections 295 to 297 and remove references to religion-related offences in sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will also make related amendments to section 74 of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Section 74 of the Penal Code currently provides for enhanced maximum punishments of up to one-and-a-half times, where a specified list of Penal Code offences is committed in a racially or religiously aggravated manner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This includes situations where the offender demonstrates hostility towards the victim based on the victim’s religion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The scope of section 74 will be expanded in two ways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will also exclude offences which have incorporated a racial aggravating factor, such as sections 298 and 298A.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Clause 17 gives effect to these amendments to the Penal Code.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These amendments are necessary to refresh our toolbox of legislative levers, so that we can continue to respond effectively to the growing threats to religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The amendments we have proposed today are testament to the Government's commitment to continue to safeguard religious harmony, which is vital to the peace and progress that we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Around the world, enmity among religious groups have created an inability for people to practise their religion in peace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some countries, practising one's faith has cost property, safety and lives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the Czech Republic, the construction of a mosque was met with petitions, street demonstrations, public hearings and vandalism to the homes of Muslim families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Stereotypes and misconceptions about Christians and Christian practices were rampant even among school children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2014, in India, altered images of Hindu kings of medieval India and a right-wing political leader sparked stone pelting, violence and damaged vehicles and religious places of a minority community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In February 2019, in the US, a synagogue's window was smashed on a Sabbath while the rabbi and his family, including young children, were inside.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2014 and 2018, in Sri Lanka, Buddhist extremists attacked Muslim Sri Lankans, spreading rumours that planted fear and insecurity as well as hate speech that caused violence and riots to break out.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Christians in Sri Lanka are also not spared.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having seen what is happening around the world, should our Government just sit by and not do anything?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or should the Government take a more proactive role in securing and protecting our precious religious harmony?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some may say that we do not need this Bill since we have never issued a single RO since the Act was passed in 1990.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the mere presence of the law does have an educative and even a deterrent effect.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just because a law is not actively used or enforced does not mean it is useless.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The virality and speed at which hate speech which harms religious harmony travel have increased greatly through the use of technology and social media.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Facebook post with altered images of venerated ancient Hindu warrior kings and a political leader is one such example.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told a Security Council Ministerial meeting that "the new frontier is cyber-terrorism – the use of social media and the dark web to coordinate attacks, spread propaganda and recruit new followers".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The threats we face are morphing and what is needed are updated tools to be able to address these potential harms.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just because there are more tools does not mean the tools need to be utilised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just as how the MRHA was not enforced these 28 years, similarly, the powers under the amended MRHA Bill we are debating today should continue to be used judiciously.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They also need to be confirmed or varied by the President per section 12.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, may I ask the Minister to explain why it is that the PCRH can recommend varying a new RO under section 11(5) whereas the power of the Council regarding an existing order is available only to confirm or cancel but not to vary it?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I ask this question in relation to the amended section 13(3).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, overall, my view is that there are safeguards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, for an RO under MRHA, not only does the PCRH need to scrutinise the RO, the President also needs to confirm it, vary, cancel or refuse to confirm it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not just provided for under section 12 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also provided for under Article 22I of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is similar to the President's discretion to concur with a Detention Order under the Internal Security Act (ISA) under Art 151(4) of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as this Bill is updated to meet the morphing threats of our times, it is important to reiterate some key principles undergirding religious freedom and the preservation of religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Article 15 of the Constitution states that every person in Singapore has the right to profess, practise and propagate his religion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Paragraph 3 of Article 15 also states that every religious group has the right to manage its own religious affairs, to establish and maintain institutions for religious or charitable purposes and to acquire and own property and hold and administer it in accordance with the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Flowing from this constitutional right, it is important that religions be given the space in Singapore to exercise those freedoms.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, freedoms must be exercised within proper boundaries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, someone cannot use the freedom as a licence to intentionally promote enmity, hatred, ill-will or hostility.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is addressed in the new section 17F(1) and (3).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is appropriate to hold leaders to a higher standard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since they wield greater influence and have others entrusted to their care, they should bear greater responsibility for their actions and words.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, there needs to be clarity as to whom this standard applies to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister clarify the scope of "religious leaders" in the Bill?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The explanatory statement states that it includes lay leaders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would that include part-time staff, those invited to speak to recount their experience and give testimonies to a religious group; counsellors who help families overcome financial, family or marriage difficulties or the loss of loved ones; those who do or organise charitable work, such as providing rations for families in the neighbourhood?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some religions require making an oath or taking certain vows or going through certain ceremonial rites.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other religions do not require such a formal commissioning process to become a leader.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some religious groups formalise mentorship or open up the facilitation of small group discussions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to prevent the spread of foreign radicalised teachings that promote violent extremism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the ways in which this objective has sought to be achieved in the Bill is by limiting the involvement of foreign persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, the good work of religious groups should not be unduly hampered by safeguards against foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Historically, religious leaders from other countries have contributed greatly to Singapore’s development.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Religious leaders from other parts of the world, such as England, Australia, Portugal, Ireland, China and India came to spread or practise their religion through charitable deeds.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They helped set up schools, hospitals, hospices, offer midwifery services, cared for the sick and wounded during the Japanese Occupation, doing good work for the communities here.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of these charitable institutions have been corporatised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, many religious groups in Singapore have links to foreign institutions, for example, the Catholic Archdiocese of Singapore with the Vatican, the Anglicans with Canterbury, Buddhist groups with Sri Lanka and Thailand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree that disclosure is needed to prevent situations where there is a deliberate intent to create enmity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also a good move to anticipate potential divisions that hate speech can create, but I hope the discretion to give exemptions will be exercised wisely, tactfully and delicately because of the universal nature of charity, honest hard work and integrity often found in religious values and organisations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to say, Sir, that there is strength when people of different religions come together to work for the common good.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was touched by a recent exercise conducted by the grassroots leaders involving porridge distribution in the constituency I serve in Ulu Pandan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rice was donated by the Singapore Buddhist Lodge, it was then cooked into delicious porridge or bubur by members of the Al Huda Mosque and then distributed by volunteers from St Ignatius Church.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, there were Christians, Muslims, Hindus and Buddhists who distributed the porridge within my constituency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We came together – different religions in Singapore – to offer the less-advantaged residents lovingly-cooked porridge.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was very meaningful for me and those present.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill was crafted and passed in 1990.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: One could argue that the fact that we never invoked the Bill shows that our society is harmonious despite our religious differences and that perhaps we could even repeal the Bill entirely.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Human societies are not static and the world has changed since 1990.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Human habits and attitudes have not changed, especially when it comes to dealing with differences and diversity.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The ability to provoke and incite violence may be as old as mankind.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And, in recent years, we continue to see violence sparked and perpetuated in the name of religion.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: So, in general, Sir, I support these amendments.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But forgive the pun, the devil is in the details.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: So, clearly, for religious leaders, given their level of influence, the bar to make their actions an offence is much lower than those of lay persons.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I have two concerns with this provision.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: In the first instance, how do we define being wounded by words of the other parties?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But what about genuine differences of opinions or views?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: After all, is religion not, by its very nature, exclusive?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: This was pointed out by the White Paper of 26 December 1989.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I adopt a certain religion because I believe it to be the truth and everything else to be untrue.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And if I utter my views about what I understand and believe to be untrue of the other religions publicly, will I be guilty of an offence?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: A similar concern could be raised for those without any religious belief but who believe that certain practices of certain religions are not right and may make public statements about it.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The bar in this case would be if it threatens public order or public peace.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: If only one person feels wounded by the words of a non-religious person expressing his or her negative views of that person’s religion, would that be a sufficient condition to deem this action an offence?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And what if the “wounded person” can claim publicly on social media that his religion has been insulted and others from his religion feel equally wounded, would that make it an offence?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Would there be any difference if 10 others, or perhaps a thousand others, express support for him online?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And in this respect, hatred could be directed towards the person who started this all.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Can that person then seek protection under the Bill as his life is now being threatened by those feeling wounded?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: This scenario I have painted is already happening on social media.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The to-ing and fro-ing of claims and counterclaims of who is right and wrong about views of religion and religious practices is likely to spark unintended consequences, even though the origins of these spats may merely stem from a difference of views and are not motivated by hate of a particular religious group.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I hope the Minister can enlighten us.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The White Paper of 1989 also raised this as an issue for the attention of our Government.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I support this, especially when we see sectarian violence in different parts of the world within the same faith community.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I am particularly concerned about the Sunni-Shia divide that is evident in some parts of the world and has found its way into the region.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We must not import the religious divides and violence of other countries into Singapore.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I have expressed my concern about this trend on other platforms and have called for better understanding between my Sunni compatriots and the Shias who, while not great in number in this part of the world, are also Muslims.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We know that there are different sects in almost every religion and there are tensions of varying degrees among groups in every religion.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: So, whether in Islam or in any other religion, I believe that religious harmony must start at home and every faith community must respect differences within their own faiths.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Article 15 of the Constitution guarantees the freedom of religion where “every person has the right to profess and practise his religion and to propagate it”.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: If I merely state the truth as I believe it to be about my religion to another person of a different faith and make claims that his religion is not true, is this considered aggressive?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, the 1989 White Paper provided many examples by different groups of what they deemed to be aggressive proselytisation.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But what about those who do it through actions which are not religiously related, like showing preferences in hiring or giving certain advantages to those from the same faith?

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The White Paper highlighted in its section on religion and politics on the need to keep the public space as secular as possible.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Interestingly, the paper also cautions that it is almost impossible for someone who is voting to base his decision on his secular half and not his religious half.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Such compartmentalisation, it notes, is “neither possible nor desirable”.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why it is absurd to ask me to decide whether I am first a Muslim or a Singaporean.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Apart from these concerns of definition and interpretation, we need to be careful about how we go about implementing or prosecuting these cases.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: A real question is at what point do we impose aggressive punishments and restrictions.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Such a posture not only protects against the stirring up of religious conflicts but sends a strong message that any attempt to incite ill-will or violence will not be tolerated.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The digital revolution has made it easy to spread extreme opinions, and such people may feel that they can be more abusive online without having to face consequences.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to send a strong signal that the harmonious relations that we have built up over the last 54 years are precious and must be guarded jealously.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Like a piece of good China, once broken, it is very difficult to put the pieces back together.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet, Sir, the need to be careful must not end up silencing all discussion of religious topics by making it such that the definitions of illegal behaviour are so ambiguous that no one can be sure what might be judged hateful.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Ironically, this might end up deterring meaningful interfaith efforts among groups as people steer away from any activity or topic for fear of causing unintended offence.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Likewise, we need to be careful not to silence civil interfaith and intrafaith conversations and debates, even about sensitive issues which can yield important insights and further deepen understandings on all sides.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The basis for religious harmony also cannot be the fear of the law.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: For religious harmony in a society to be strong and enduring, the citizenry must uphold the values of mutual respect and appreciation towards religious diversity.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: In this regard, in Singapore, educational efforts as well as outreach toward youth and community groups enable people to better understand the beliefs of religious groups and to forge friendships across communities.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: All these efforts must continue and be strengthened.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Where there are transgressions, providing platforms and avenues whereby religious groups respond and confront hateful views with arguments and information remain important.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Mistrust among the different faith communities can lead to the breaking up of our society.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a need for this legislation in dealing with those planning to split the communities in Singapore.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, in such cases, the Government could consider a range of engagement efforts involving leaders from all the communities involved to resolve the dispute.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: So, let us not be quick to condemn the slightest provocation as it could all be a simple misunderstanding.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I understand this exclusion stems from the practical difficulties in policing all corners of Singapore.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet, the best restraint must come from all of us.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: What we believe is the right thing to say in public must also be the right thing to say privately.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: What underpins our behavior publicly and privately must be the belief that what all Singaporeans hold dear as their faith deserves to be respected, irrespective of our own beliefs and faith.

speaker: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Having said that, it must be the desire of all our faith groups and leaders that we interact freely with grace and mutual respect, without the need for the law to kick in.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It protects our religious freedom, by making clear the boundaries of our mutual engagements.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Since then, the world around us has evolved and changed.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Globalisation has increased our connectedness with foreign cultures and communities; social media has transformed how we communicate; hate speech and violence in the name of personal beliefs and faiths are on the rise.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore is not immune to these trends, and they threaten the religious harmony that we have spent decades carefully tending.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government is not alone in holding this view.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I chair the National Steering Committee on Racial and Religious Harmony, whose members comprise apex leaders from the major faith and ethnic groups.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have built a strong foundation for social cohesion in Singapore, which we must vigorously safeguard.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have proven that our communities can come together to discuss sensitive issues of race and religion seriously, candidly but respectfully, with the common goal of making Singapore a better home for everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is the case whenever we discuss religious radicalisation activities, or when we discuss results of studies on race and religion in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It was the same when we debated the introduction of the Reserved Presidential Election.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It was also the same when we debated the ban of the Swedish black metal band Watain from performing in Singapore, because the band advocated violence against a religion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It demonstrated the desire of our people for a cohesive society that will deal with such emotive issues publicly, transparently and calmly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Although we are here to debate on the Bill, laws alone do not bring about the cohesive society that I have described.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Legislative solutions cannot address the many challenges that we face.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, although we can implement policies, such as the Ethnic Integration Policy, we cannot legislate neighbours to interact with others of different faiths.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our schools cannot dictate that classmates must eat and play together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At a more fundamental level, we cannot legislate to remove irrational fears and stereotypes, nor to accept that a set of different beliefs can coexist with ours.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In other words, legislation, though important, is not sufficient.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our social harmony has been built painstakingly over time.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is through individual actions and efforts in our everyday lives to engage one another.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This requires continued effort and we, as Singaporeans, must all do our part.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This was emphasised 30 years ago, in the original 1989 White Paper on Maintenance of Religious Harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I quote, “So long as all Singaporeans understand that they have to live and let live, and show respect and tolerance for other faiths, harmony should prevail”.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Underlying this is a shared commitment to build a home together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is a home built on the ideal of a multiracial and multi-religious society where everyone has the freedom to choose and practise his or her religion, provided the same freedom is afforded to others.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When Singapore became independent, our founding fathers made a deliberate choice to build our nation based on such a multiracial, multi-religious society, as an expression of what Singapore stands for.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It was a novel idea at the time when most newly-independent countries opted to entrench a dominant race, language and religion, because it was the easier and primordial path.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is done out of a tribal instinct to protect its identity and ensure its existence.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Multiculturalism, of sharing the societal space with all races, on the other hand, has become an integral part of our Singapore identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All of us want a society where all Singaporeans, regardless of background, feel that they are equal members of the same community.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The social compact will allow us to broaden our common space, even as our society becomes more diverse.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We, the Government, are committed to working with Singaporeans, at all levels, to safeguard racial and religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have remained steadfast in this approach since our beginnings.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The People’s Association was set up in 1960, with promoting social cohesion and connecting people from all walks of life as one of its main objectives.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Grassroots organisations help to resolve local issues and bridge communities through dialogue and engagement.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Today, IRCC members help resolve local issues that may arise from time to time, work on projects jointly, such as emergency preparedness, and help one another.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: During this year’s Hari Raya Haji, a Buddhist organisation helped to manage traffic for a neighbouring mosque so that its prayer service could run smoothly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This idea arose during an IRCC meeting and was carried out by IRCC members.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We support efforts by religious and community leaders to promote racial and religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This Declaration is still recited at interfaith events.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government helped facilitate multiple engagement sessions with a wide group of religious leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Dozens of secular community organisations, companies, social service agencies and educational institutions have also expressed support for this.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ground-up efforts to promote racial and religious harmony are rising.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several community groups have facilitated candid and open dialogues on race and religion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, The WhiteHatters organised a series of conversations called Ask Me Anything (AMA) where participants of diverse faiths engage religious leaders to clarify their understanding of their religions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In June, the organisers brought together the Christian, Jewish and Muslim representatives to discuss the Abrahamic faiths.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In September, OnePeople.sg collaborated with Channel NewsAsia and Roses of Peace, a non-governmental organisation, to conduct dialogue sessions on race relations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Inter-Religious Organisation (IRO), in conjunction with its 70th anniversary, held a Harmony of Faiths exhibition that showcased efforts in promoting interfaith understanding throughout its years.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Beyond programmes, more Singaporeans are also expressing interest and respect for diversity in our daily lives.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the workplace, management plays an important role in creating a conducive work environment for a diverse workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These have helped strengthen understanding among its employees and enhanced the contributions of the diverse teams.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More companies should, similarly, pay attention to building race and religious competency.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We grew to appreciate what we have in common and how our differences make us richer, not poorer.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Today, we harness our diversity as our strength, and we are a society with genuine friendships built on goodwill, trust and confidence in what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: During my recent house visits, a Chinese resident, who is a Christian, shared with me how her Muslim neighbour would help watch after her young child whenever she has to fetch another from school and her Hindu neighbour on the other side would share food with her from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And their children would often be found in one another’s homes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The resident brought this to my attention because she truly appreciated the kindness and generosity of her neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But above all, she knows that this relationship transcending differences in race and religion is not to be taken for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Such trusting and warm relationships among neighbours of different faiths can be found all around Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is the beauty of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must continue to uphold our values and keep working hard to preserve social harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must ensure that this is in the DNA of every Singaporean, so that we remain as one united people regardless of language, race and religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, it is important to remember the sociopolitical context of 30 years ago, when the Bill was first debated in the House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
