text: Generally, that era was known to be a time of heightened religiosity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bill was mooted only about one month after the detention of some Singaporeans who were accused of being Marxists.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is important, if not critical, to note that the passage of the underlying Act in 1990 itself did not go without significant apprehension from religious groups and Members of Parliament, including differences of opinion amongst even Ministers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even Mr Shanmugam's speech, in his capacity as a backbencher then, was noteworthy because it raised fundamental points about the separation of powers and the potential for an irrational exercise of Executive power.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prime Minister Lee, in his capacity as Minister of Trade and Industry and the then-Minister of National Development, Mr S Dhanabalan, both disagreed about the interplay between politics and religion in special situations where religious bodies would have no choice but to get involved in politics to overthrow a government, for example, in the event the government turns corrupt, oppressive, tyrannical.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Marxist arrests clouded the passage of the Act somewhat then, this Government today is not similarly encumbered insofar as the amendments to the Bill are concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Racial harmony remains a critical and important national value that must be upheld alongside the spirit of tolerance among believers of all religious groups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the political narrative that has been developing within our closest neighbours, Indonesia, Malaysia and even regionally in Southern Thailand, while strictly speaking is not our business, is nonetheless cause for concern.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The recent Indonesian Presidential Elections also saw candidates speaking to burnish their religious credentials.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And with social media, it has become a more sensitive matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, this is something the Government and politicians and political party members of all political parties in Singapore need to keep an eye on as well in view of our unique context and political circumstances and consider whether there may be some things that have to be tightened.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With a difficult subject – the mixing of religion and politics – at the heart of the Act, the signals a one-party dominant government and its politicians send on the subject will have a direct bearing on how the Act will be applied and deemed relevant in years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will spend the first part of my speech to share some examples about how things can be perceived on the ground in Singapore, in spite of the spirit of the underlying Act which seeks to keep religions and politics separate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A well-known leader of a religious group fronting many national initiatives, including being a very senior party member and highly visible leader of the IRO and separately with links to the People's Association was seen with Prime Minister Lee during the 2015 elections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While it is unclear if the individual concerned was the Prime Minister's election agent, it is nonetheless useful for the House to pause and consider the optics of a respected member of a religious group appearing to canvass support for a politician.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, how would some members of the same religious group with a different political view from that espoused by their religious leader or elder feel if they openly support another political party?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could it create or ferment tension within that religious group?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should another group or individual from within any particular religious organisation or faith rise in stature because of a disagreement or internal politics, would it be fair game for a politician from another party to canvass support for him or her?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What can we reasonably foresee may happen next?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, we should pause and consider the effect of politicians of all political parties attending places of worship of any faith as political leaders, as opposed to just lay congregants, visitors or well-wishers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, even events that take place in this House can be open to close scrutiny and test the long-held approach of the state as a neutral arbiter when it comes to matters of faith.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the first Sitting that took place in this House following the tragic mosque shootings in Christchurch in March this year, this House observed a moment of silence for the victims of that massacre.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Only a mere month later, many Christians perished in Sri Lanka in a series of suicide bombings there.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that some Christian Singaporeans privately wondered why Parliament did not observe a moment of silence for those Christians who perished in Sri Lanka as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would more religious or quasi-religious invitations or relationships between the state and citizens be better managed through the unifying and ceremonial role of the President or some other platform?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is something the Government would need to assess and consider carefully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With no prospect of judicial review to adjudicate the rationality of executive fiat, clarity in how the law is applied and impartiality from the Government is paramount, not just in words but in action.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if they publicly raise objections or disagreements about Government policy, in line with the Second Reading of the Act in 1990, the MRHA portends that action could be taken against them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What the perception of such a one-way conversation or approach would ultimately do is to undermine and damage the Government’s case if it seeks to use the Act in future to move against elements that it deems to be mixing religion and politics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As we look towards tomorrow’s Singapore, and as we enter the fourth generation (4G) era, this House must ensure that the public space continues to be a secular and safe space for all Singaporeans, regardless of creed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the terrain of religion and politics is not without its difficulties, it is critical that restraint, mutual respect and equanimity define how both politicians and religious leaders operate in Singapore where being a successful multiracial and multi-religious society is a significant value proposition in our neighbourhood and for our survival as one people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Whatever our political views, religion can be exploited and the use of religion to split communities is a renewed concern, given the advent of fast-moving communications technology.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But when they threaten the multiracial harmony of our society, the Government needs to step in to protect our hard-won harmony.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: MRHA has served us well in preserving the peace and harmony in our multiracial society.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we need to update the law to reflect the current needs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The media has exposed how many users of the Internet have used it to promote hidden agendas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Today, there are also less scrupulous religious groups that use these platforms to attack, disrupt and spread extremist views or hostility towards other religions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And we know how a post on the Internet can go viral rapidly, especially when it relates to sensational topics.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot afford to wait 14 days or more to allow ROs to kick in for the offending online content to be removed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister consider penalties for those who deliberately circulate such offending content, especially if they are influential pages?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While I agree that these acts have potentially serious consequences that deserve heavy penalties, things like wounding religious feelings can be rather subjective.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, it may simply be due to misunderstanding or clashing cultures and no ill will was truly intended.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has consulted with religious groups in enacting this Bill and I hope they will continue to consult with the relevant religious groups when applying the laws, too, as well as conduct dialogues with relevant stakeholders and affected parties after the laws are applied.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The end goal should be to determine why certain acts are deemed offensive and how to prevent them from happening in future.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After all, many offences happen as a result of a lack of empathy and ignorance, rather than pure malice.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope we can nurture a society that is more sympathetic but act decisively when the need arises.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In previous cases, some people who insulted other races and religions were doxxed and had their livelihoods affected, with some even losing their jobs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we can rehabilitate criminals, can we do the same for cases under MRHA?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Religion has a huge impact and influence on many.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, there is reasonable cause for concern over foreigners taking advantage of this fact to try to abuse religion to establish their own agenda.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, for smaller organisations, this requirement may be hard to meet.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the Government is willing to grant exemptions on a case-by-case basis, or for cross-border or historical organisations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For foreign appointment holders who get exemptions, it may be good for them to be given some basic education on the framework of our religious harmony practices so that they know the consequences if they breach the MRHA law.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   With the advancement of communication technologies, foreign groups and social media will have an increasing influence on our religious groups.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, they may bring in views that could damage religious harmony here.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, the amendments this time are targeted at these two areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, what is considered as an insult to other religions can be subjective.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I hope the Government can consult religious leaders first before banning certain types of remarks, and hold dialogues with relevant religious groups after the enforcement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am also pleased to see that the Government can order the offenders to understand other religions or issue a public apology.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a more proactive way of correcting wrong views besides banning.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, for smaller religious groups, it may be a tall order.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can make decisions on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If foreigners are to become key personnel, they must first attend lessons to understand the principles of maintaining religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill gives us the opportunity to ask if we share the same consensus today, in a globalised world where religious ideas, for good or ill, flow as easily across borders as trade does, and where people feel affinity with religious and social causes far away.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While religious Singaporeans can be proud that they share the faith with brethren in many countries, we must have a consensus that the practice of faith here must be sensitive to our own multi-religious context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If so, then we must accept that the state must have some means of enforcing this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the New Testament, Jesus was asked whether Jews should pay taxes to the Roman authorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: He responded that they should "render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s." It is legitimate for the practice of religion to adapt to the requirements of the secular state and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: All religions have a right to make rules of moral and ethical conduct that followers are expected to live up to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But when these rules of conduct contrast with secular law, or with the established norms of society, then the proponents of any religion face a hard decision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Do they seek to explain why the way of life prescribed in the religion is superior, more ethical or moral, to persuade those who wandered astray to return to the fold?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Or do they condemn such behaviours, portray those who have lapsed as sinners, encourage followers to ostracise or ex-communicate those who do not live according to their principles?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We may disagree with some of their precepts but not their commitment to bettering humanity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must caution against the condemnation of our fellow Singaporeans simply based on behaviour which strays from the precepts of a particular religion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And we must be cautious even when such criticism applies only to co-religionists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nearly every religion is concerned with the nature of the family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are rules for marriage and separation, proper sexual relations and other family affairs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Women can, and do, live independent of men today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A divorcee or widow is no longer condemned to penury or forced into a second marriage by society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While many different types of family relationships exist, I believe all aspire to having a happy family life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The state may have some interest in it to promote social order and the national interest, but this interest cannot and must never be religiously motivated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The exception, of course, is Muslim Law for the family life of Muslims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the general policy must be secular in a multi-religious society like Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But this position that the state should refrain from interfering with private family life is at odds with the position taken by many great religions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, religious leaders in many countries routinely demand changes in family policy so that religious principles are enforced with the full weight of the state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They do so either because, in those countries, the right of free speech is nearly absolute, or because there is a state religion and hence there is little difference between theology and public policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Their situation is not the same as in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This right, if applied indiscriminately in Singapore, would lead to the shrinking of the secular space in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The language used has, sometimes, been alarmist and unaccommodating.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Again, Sir, I support the right of every religion to prescribe principles of life for their followers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I hope religious leaders will promote their precepts constructively, rather than destructively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that they will speak to our common humanity, rather than divide us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans who disturb the religious peace accept that they are in the wrong and they voluntarily change their ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Indiscriminate use of the law would create contention rather than consensus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The significant expansion of powers under this Bill raises that risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While this Government has demonstrated that moral suasion and dialogue are the preferred tools to enforce the law, I pray that a future Government will also respect that wise precedent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With revivalism of religious faith in the 1980s, the Government and society in general have been concerned with how religious fervour may prove to be fertile ground for fanaticism or radicalism.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The late 1980s and the early 1990s saw numerous incidents that were cited in the Internal Security Department’s (ISD's) report that was annexed to the White Paper proposing the enactment of MRHA.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Examples of aggressive and insensitive proselytisation, of intra-religious sectarianism, as well as issues of the use of faith for political ends are still as important today as they were when MRHA was first formulated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Equally, the concerns on the reach of MRHA that were raised when the law took effect in 1992 also remain today and should be rightly addressed so that we are without a doubt of the pure and noble intent of this Bill, which is, to safeguard the harmony of Singapore that we have fought hard to build.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They include lines such as: "Patriotic Church much like China", "Will we ban fasting, too?", "Aggressive atheism in disguise", "All religious heads must now be pro-Government".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I must hasten to add that while these are minority views, a few come from level-headed people who I know.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would perhaps say that if not for this amendment Bill, there would be many who would not be aware of the content of MRHA to begin with.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the plans that MHA have to engage people of faith as well as the society at large?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Religions like Islam and Christianity are what some would term as holistic religions, ones where adherents follow a code of life that is all-encompassing, where participation in the political life of society is informed by faith as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Section 8(1)(b) and (d) were points of concern in 1990.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It may be helpful today to state clearly what would constitute offences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would it, therefore, be an offence if, in the event that the Government of the day enacts or proposes a law that would run counter to the core tenets or beliefs of an established religion or religions in Singapore, and religious leaders of those faiths issue a public letter to their faithful or preach a message against it, against the intent of the law, I must add, and not the Government itself?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would it constitute something that an RO will be issued against as the message – even though religious and measured in nature – may cause some members of the congregation to be dissatisfied?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would it constitute a political cause in this case?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, while the Government is accommodatively secular, allowing religions to function and practise freely in Singapore, we cannot guarantee that a future Government will not become aggressively atheistic and, therefore, apply MRHA beyond what it was originally drafted for.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Returning to a point I made earlier about how the Act is being more responsive, as pointed out by a number of political officeholders who spoke when the Bill was introduced, the key component of the Act will now be able to respond to the alarming speed by which hate speech and fake news can spread on social media, and how something inflammatory that may have been a slow boil during the 1990s can now heat up in the web in mere minutes and translate to real, explosive tensions offline.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I last spoke about how Singapore can easily be a target for disinformation operations because of our openness and connectivity during the Second Reading on POFMA.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over one third of the world is on Facebook alone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Much of how we interact with one another today is through social media.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a majority of the world moves into the unfettered online world, it also means old tropes of racism, misogyny and hate now have a free amplifier to spread and reinforce their views and perhaps even encourage others to violence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Ministry share with the House how, in practice, the new powers granted would improve the effectiveness of curbing the spread of speech that would incite hatred?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, what recourse by which those who have been issued an RO can seek redress if they truly believe that they have expressed a legitimate view and not hate speech?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to POFMA, how will MRHA interface with it so that we have a seamless process to target fake news, hate speech and rumour-mongering?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is heartening that in proposing the amendments, MHA has consulted broadly, and the apex organisations of religious groups in Singapore have accepted and supported the proposals.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I applaud the Bill’s innovativeness, especially for the introduction of CRI.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As mentioned by Minister Shanmugam earlier, it has taken fruit even before we passed this amendment, from the recent example of a young influencer who accepted the invitation of the Young Sikh Association to learn more about their faith and traditions after posting an insensitive social media comment about two Sikh men she encountered at an event.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I agree with the need to prevent foreign influence in Singapore but am cautious about how we would qualify “foreign influence” in practice.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The amendments proposed restrictions on the leadership appointments of religious organisations and donations, for example.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the appointment of religious leaders is complex.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most religions are universal by nature, belonging to global networks, alliances and associations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some, like particular Buddhist sects and Roman Catholicism, or different denominations in Christianity, have global leaderships.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How would the Act, in practice, address the peculiarities of some leadership appointments that may involve a global or external decision?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Minister provide examples of organisations that would be required to seek exemptions?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What would happen to these organisations should the exemptions not be provided?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Act also become a prohibition for the entrance of new religious movements or denominations and sects if they do not already have a local presence?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore is fortunate as an example of a country that has bucked the trend of racial and religious tensions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just looking at a recent Pew Research Centre survey makes for cold sweat.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this research, it points out the percentage of people who agree that people should be able to make statements that are offensive to minority groups publicly, and this was done in just 2015.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the US, 67% of people agree that they should be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the Asia Pacific, in which Singapore is situated, 27% or close to 30% of people, believe that they should be allowed to make inflammatory statements that are offensive to minority groups publicly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The two principles stated were: first, that followers of different religions should exercise moderation and tolerance towards each other and their beliefs, and not instigate religious enmity and hatred; and secondly, that religion and politics should be kept separate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The debate on any curtailment of religious freedom is difficult because our Constitution guarantees freedom of religion as a fundamental liberty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Article 15(1) provides that every person has the right to profess and practise his religion and to propagate it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, it is a fundamental right of a person not only to believe in the god he chooses, but to manifest that belief in action, and to spread the belief to non-believers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today's debate is really one about the extent of this right.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans value the peaceful co-existence of multiple religions in Singapore, and the Workers' Party values this as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the weekend, I visited the home of a resident who was obviously a devout follower of his faith.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I asked him about his views on other faiths, he said, "I believe what I believe, not because you are wrong, but because my god is the right god for me." Singaporeans, on the whole, embody a spirit of moderation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, we agree that the agenda setting in religious matters should be done by Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has expressed concern that some foreign brands of religiosity, if imported, may not be appropriate and may cause tensions on religious grounds to arise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There have been news reports that the major religious groups in Singapore support these amendments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It could be argued by some that the powers in the Bill constitute an erosion of the autonomy of religious groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in his Second Reading speech, the Minister did say that it was not the intention of the Government to constrain the practice of religion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it is important for the Ministry to further elaborate on why the Government believes that the Bill is fully consistent with Article 15.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although this Bill does not specifically deal with the separation of religion and politics, it is useful to remind ourselves of what the separation of religion and politics entails.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is especially timely, in view of the impending General Election.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the debate on the Act 30 years ago, it was acknowledged that it is not possible to strictly divorce religion from politics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This impossibility is true today and probably for all ages.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Like Mr Alex Yam before me, I am a Catholic myself and I am to be guided by the Church’s teachings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The tenets of Christianity exhort Christians to promote social justice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Biblical book of the prophet Isaiah, it is written: “Seek justice, encourage the oppressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Defend the case of the fatherless, plead the case of the widow”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Advocacy for the voiceless is every Christian’s calling.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a force for good in Singapore as we address concerns about class divides and move to foster an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, while individuals may order their actions based on their faiths, the picture takes on a more sensitive hue when religious leaders openly champion social or political causes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has previously voiced its concern about the possible misuse of religious authority.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the focus of today’s Bill is on foreign interference, we should be vigilant that Singapore’s own religious leaders do not polarise their congregations along party political lines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this, I wish to share some observations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the run-up to the debate on this Bill, there has been open support for the Bill expressed by religious leaders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Religious authority is being thrown behind the Government’s legislation, both publicly and also to specific congregations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as I know, the Government has welcomed this open support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But if the religious leaders had instead gone the other way, that is, express concern or opposition to the Bill, would the Government have put its foot down and issued an order requiring them to stop?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Or is it right for a religious leader to be publicly seen walking into a Nomination Centre in party uniform with a political party’s candidates on Nomination Day?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is already brewing on the ground that some religious institutions are developing reputations for being supportive of certain political parties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Any decision by religious leaders to take an openly partisan stance bears the risk of causing tension between followers who ascribe to their leaders’ political allegiances and those who do not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The MRHA was controversial at the time it was passed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: By restricting foreign influence on our religious institutions, we also allow our national and religious identities to intersect more closely.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last, this Bill is built for speed, given the very large harm that can result from religious insult within a very short time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I see this Bill as one among a slew of others to protect our rights and the kind of society we have pledged to be.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Singapore model of protecting rights has always been one that relies on restrictions of freedoms, in an explicit recognition that rights without restrictions are empty.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If everyone is completely free to do whatever we want, then we yield our individual freedoms to those with the most power, which, in modern society, has tended to be those with the most wealth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Countries which we consider to be democratic today are perhaps merely plutocracy well-disguised.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I give two examples of laws which appear to trample on freedoms but yet provides the most freedoms for the most of us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Land Acquisition Act is recognition that the rights of private property owners are sometimes subordinate to the claims of the state.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The ethnic quota guideline in our public housing estate is evidence that the right to freely transact on the market is conscribed by the larger goals of racial harmony through the everyday lived experience of all races.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The restriction of hate speech is the latest in a series of these, a vital link in preserving the high quality of public discourse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Each restriction of vital freedoms is not to deny that such freedoms are important but is our way of recognising that such freedoms exist within a universe of rights.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, it is morally wrong, that is, wrong in principle; second, it has the potential to cause great harm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And it is this latter which carves out the three main areas which the current legislation addresses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hate speech divides us, sets man against man, tribe against tribe; it stirs us up, it inflates and inflames our emotions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, and on the other end of the spectrum, it dampens our responses to and normalises outrageous behaviour.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What may once have given us pause may now be shrugged off and accepted.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this way, we lose our collective public morality.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And he pointed out the dangers of allowing hate speech to move into the mainstream.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He said, and I quote him, "With each broken norm, the pillars of humanity are weakened." We cannot allow the norms of Singapore to become so lax that hate against one another's religion goes unpunished by law.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Third, hate speech moves individuals to take radical action.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the name of overweening but ultimately false causes, we have seen Nazis against Jews during the Holocaust, Hutus against Tutsis in Rwanda, Sinhalese Buddhists against minorities in Sri Lanka.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is also the long-standing risk, with terrorist groups calling on Muslims to establish an Islamic caliphate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He said, "All these ideas are new ideas, which are ideas from old texts or interpretation of old texts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, these need to be addressed by our own scholars." So, what can we do against the force of religious beliefs?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the UK, it is a crime to incite hatred on the grounds of religion.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But it protects freedom of expression to a high degree, to such an extent that one can ridicule and insult, abuse any religion or its followers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Like many countries, Singapore finds hate speech wrong in principle.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Like some of these countries, Singapore is willing to use the strongest institution at our disposal – our laws – to bind this wrong because of the harm it does to our society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, we are nesting it within an ecosystem of laws that promote a high quality of public life and discourse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods, which I was a member of, heard expert advice which argues that the "visible hand" of the state is needed to fight fake news.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Lies mixed with religious fervour presents an explosive cocktail.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, our willingness to give force to this "invisible hand".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not always the case, In some countries, something can be recognised to be wrong and harmful but still remain unbound either because there is a lack of political will or because it lies outside the political culture.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, we recognise that in our best selves, we can rise above our primordial instincts, we can forbear from rash, unreasoned action, we listen to others, we can be dispassionate and rational.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But let us not be conceited enough to think that we are our best selves all the time, or even most of the time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Let us not be naive to think that what happened in history cannot and will not happen again.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There will always be critics who say that yes, they agree that religious harmony is important, but we should not be so ready to make new laws.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We should trim our legal reach and give more respect and freedoms to the citizens.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To do otherwise is to disrespect the ability of citizens to hold mature political dialogue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Sir, MRHA was enacted in 1992.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But before that, I would like to seek a clarification from the Minister on one new section being introduced which can be found in this amendment Bill, which is section 17(F).

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I will share an example, and I hope that the Minister can provide a clarification, based on the example given, whether an offence had taken place as stated under section 17 in the following situation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: An Islamic religious leader or preacher said during a sermon that Islam teaches that Jesus was a prophet and not the son of God as taught in Christianity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He then says that any religion that says otherwise that Jesus is the son of God, then the followers of that religion will be punished in hell.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While delivering the sermon, the preacher also delivers that message in a fervent manner.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If a video recording of that session is shared on the Internet, I think it is very likely that the majority of Christians will feel offended and angry because they feel that the preacher has insulted their faith.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, from the perspective of the preacher, his intention was simply to deliver Islamic teachings to Muslims and he had no intention or motive to injure anyone's feelings or cause any friction in a multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There is constant emphasis on messages stating moderation and tolerance as key elements to achieve integration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Every religion directs its followers to work towards achieving and maintaining racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that every religion calls for moderation and tolerance for the sake of harmony amongst humankind.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But, Sir, what is the meaning of moderation and tolerance in religion?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Do moderation and tolerance mean that the followers of a religion have to compromise their religious values and practices, like making themselves "less Islamic" and so on?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Do the followers of a particular religion have to do something prohibited or that contravenes the values and teachings of the religion before he can be considered as someone who practises moderation and tolerance?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Personally, I believe that tolerance, as a pillar of religious harmony in a plural society like Singapore, is achievable without having to sacrifice the values and faith of any follower.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In short, there is no need to be less Islamic.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I was amazed by the way Australian society practises tolerance by respecting the beliefs and teachings of a religion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My father's friend, Mr A, sent his daughter to a renowned public secondary school for girls in Melbourne.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Mr A sought permission from the school to allow his daughter to practise Islam by wearing an attire that covers her modesty based on Islamic teachings.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The school allowed Mr A's daughter to wear the tudung.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In fact, his daughter was also allowed to wear long-sleeve blouses and loose-fitting clothes which, nevertheless, still comply with the school's uniform requirements in terms of colour and pattern.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Although Australia is a multi-ethnic country where its people come from all over the world, they still adhere to their country's principle of religious freedom.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a nation and a plural society, they recognise the need to respect the teachings and beliefs of followers from various regions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They do not practise tolerance by asking followers of a religion to compromise their faith or "to be less Islamic" for the sake of integration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Instead, tolerance is practised in Australia by respecting the beliefs and principles of a religion and by taking steps to render support so that the religious practices of any follower of religion are not impacted, which was what took place in the example I just shared.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I do not quite agree with this principle.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a Muslim, Islam is understood as a way of life.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Islam encompasses all aspects of life, including politics and the way to practise politics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And I understand that Christianity also believes that it is unlikely that religion can be separated from politics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe such a thing is prohibited in any religious teaching.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because religion is meant to shape individuals who are morally upright and pure of heart so that he can contribute as best as he can towards the development of society and nation, and not to use it for one's own interests or certain interests.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Each member of society must strive to give mutual respect to other faiths and to practise true tolerance in order to maintain and further strengthen religious harmony in our nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was meant to inculcate national consciousness and patriotism in schools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The then Minister for Education, Mr Ong Pang Boon, sent two drafts worked out by his Ministry's staff to the late Mr S Rajaratnam, then Minister for Foreign Affairs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Rajaratnam believed that language, race and religion were potentially divisive factors, and the pledge emphasised that these differences could be overcome if we stay united as a country.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He believed that the pledge emerged against the backdrop of a struggle to forge a sense of nationhood and to build “a Singapore we are proud of”.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Every now and then, in the papers, things happen that reflect very vividly the complexities of race and religious tensions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The changes to MRHA are timely as they deal with the complex trends the world and Singapore are currently facing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The rolling news flows in the global village have given race and religious phenomena increased visibility and potency.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, attacks against Christians in Pakistan or against Muslims in India, new incidents of anti-Semitism in Western Europe and hate crimes against Muslims in the US or Europe immediately take on a global dimension.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The worldwide ripples of these incidents have vividly underscored the sensitivity of religious issues in the global village.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is even more critical now, compared to 50 over years ago, and Singapore must safeguard itself against these changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I do have a couple of clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the distinction between private and public speech and foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If someone had secretly videotaped the speech and then propagate it, the harm would still have been done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The speaker must still be as culpable as the propagator because he had spoken the words.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It matters because when everything is viewed starkly in black and white and no one is given the chance to make amends, mistrust flourishes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It splits communities down religious fault lines even more starkly than ever.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Once communities are divided in this way, tensions will spill over quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The connection between religious tolerance and stable societies is clear.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, the question remains: how many times will we allow a person who makes religiously intolerant comments to participate in this initiative?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even though inflammatory comments can be removed online, this digital age ensures that the impact is immediate and long lasting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, it is encouraging to note that our youths clearly care about religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was nearly unanimous among the 18- to 25-year-old Singaporean respondents in the same survey that it was either unacceptable or very unacceptable for religious leaders to make insensitive comments on other religions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, the very same younger netizens might also guard online spaces more vigorously through accepting views of different nature, even though these views might seem offensive to some.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we better bring about awareness amongst our youths that while people can express their views, they should also be cognisant that some discourses should not be accorded a platform, especially in multiracial and multi-religious Singapore, that the enhancement of this Act is not the restriction of what they can say, but it is for the pursuit of higher ideals? “Regardless of race, language or religion” cannot be words recited daily in our National Pledge for a brief moment in the morning and then conveniently ignored for the remainder of the day.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Let us always remember that Singapore worked hard to lay the foundation for religious harmony and maintain it over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The timely changes to this Act are welcomed as they deal with the nuanced, complex trends in this world today.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The target group was elaborated in unambiguous terms in the Explanatory Statement on page 77 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I quote, "the target group need not be confined to persons who practise a certain religion.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is, indeed, an important change that signals the coming of age of a progressive and inclusive society that we are and must be.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I recall the 2016 case of a Singaporean man who threatened to "open fire" at the LGBTQ community in a Facebook community based on certain religious beliefs and was subsequently charged for "making an electronic record containing an incitement to violence".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the last three to six months alone, a community project I co-founded called A Good Space has been approached by three different groups who support people who suffer from mental distress because of religious discrimination.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Some call this religious trauma which is sometimes defined as when religion has been weaponised to cause guilt, shame and a feeling of unworthiness in people.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One of these groups was set up four years ago to address religious trauma for young girls and the group has supported a range of issues that were raised from micro-aggression with remarks like "your skirt’s too short, too tight", "why aren’t you in a hijab", to outright sexual harassment and violations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another is an interfaith group that was set up last year by a 35-year-old man and his wife.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He shared his traumatic experiences of deep religious indoctrination, peer pressure, pastoral surveillance and being asked to participate in the many disciplinary actions that his church did to those who were not faithful.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He eventually became, in his words, an "evangeliser climbing the church ladder who have lost my identity, my education and all other passions".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Now, his group brings together, and support, many pro-pluralistic believers regularly to share with one another their experiences of religious trauma.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another community practitioner, in her 30s, who set up a healing group in December 2016 to support Muslim women from the LGBTQ community just shared this story with me.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She attended a parenting talk by a psychologist recently at a mosque and was shocked to hear the speaker tell parents to treat their LGBTQ children like drug addicts and also encouraged them to put these children through conversion therapy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Despite a large body of scientific evidence showing that being LGBTQ is normal and healthy, and the World Health Organization having removed homosexuality as a disease 42 years ago in 1977, punishments are still imposed by religious communities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Both religion and spirituality can have a positive impact on mental health which is the basis for harmony and peace in our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But we cannot and must not dismiss the religious hurt and victims of religious abuse in this effort towards religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the new provisions will go some way in deterring these practices.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Open dialogue about such emotionally-harming practices needs to take place more often.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There needs to be more support for those affected by religious trauma.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad to see interfaith groups like Interverse by Saiful Anuar emerging in this area and hope to see more religious and interfaith communities take on such support roles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also hope that the Government proactively encourages intra-faith dialogue beyond just interfaith ones to maintain not just religious harmony but also the mental well-being of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For the Bill to truly work in achieving religious harmony as its intent, its implementation should heavily engage various religious groups.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister can decide without affected persons and religious groups nor relevant stakeholders consulting and advising on the Order.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned that the lack of notice and consultation may not sufficiently take into account the sensitivities of religious issues and the need to ensure good governance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A decision that is made without notice nor consultation may be seen as heavy-handed and controlling of the religious landscape in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The absence of consultation may also mean that the Minister has less information to decide whether making an Order is the best way to achieve religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the current Government may believe itself to be competent in making Orders appropriately, we may not be able to say the same of future governments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is important to keep the safeguard procedures of notice and consultation to ensure that the law is properly enforced.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, Mr Speaker, allowing swift issuance of the Order is efficient but may not be appropriate in all instances.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For online communications, such a swift issuance may be more suitable.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, for ROs relating to not accepting, returning or disposing of donations and the composition of the governing body, these are decisions that can be undertaken less urgently.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And to enlighten us with the implementation and training guidelines for the "competent authority" with these new provisions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As much as we enhance our laws to protect against religious intolerance, how can we also ensure that engaging in honest dialogue made in good faith for the purpose of intellectual and spiritual advancement will not make a person liable under the Act and other related legislation like the section 298 and section 298A of the Penal Code and the Sedition Act?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: New Zealand’s version of this code reads, I quote, "It is not an offence against this section to express in good faith and in decent language, or to attempt to establish by arguments used in good faith and conveyed in decent language, any opinion whatever on any religious subject." This ensures that highly intolerant segments of society who deliberately take offence will not be able to silence reasonable and well-intended speech.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Non-religious individuals in Singapore can feel restrained providing a fair response to religiously-motivated opinions for fear of causing offence, even if unintentional.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Religious harmony, which is the intent of this Bill, cannot be complete if we do not actively invite and include all the non-religious in our current interfaith initiatives.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Humanist Society Singapore had to insert itself in interfaith programmes through its assiduous efforts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Five years ago, they had to intently knock on the doors of initiatives, such as the Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) conference, National University of Singapore (NUS) interfaith, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) Paths, UnConference, RosesOfPeace, the Centre for Interfaith Understanding (CIFU), OnePeople.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Someone once said that, "Diversity is having a seat at the table.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusion is having a voice at the table.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And belonging is being heard at the table." The Bill recognises the need for us to protect our vulnerable and minority groups and is a step in the right direction by bringing them to the table.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we must do more to make sure we give everyone a voice to be heard, whether they be those who suffer from religious trauma, LGBTQ persons, atheists, unwed mothers, foreign workers, new citizens and many more minorities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because religious diversity may be a given but religious harmony, whether inter or intra, is not.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A top-down approach may risk creating merely facades without sentiment and could, in fact, perpetuate the divisions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must go beyond mere proclamations of peaceful co-existence to develop the ability to understand and communicate with one another across all kinds of divisions, within and between religions and cultures, as a fundamental prerequisite for our society to remain cohesive and robust.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government must not over-regulate peace and harmony or intervene too early as it might rob us of the opportunity, as a people, to develop this ability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This intercultural competence, and not merely multiculturalism, must be a collective responsibility and priority for a Singapore that citizens from communities can call home, truly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The community recognises the importance of practising one’s religion in a way that is respectful towards those who may profess a different belief from oneself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Singapore is a successful, thriving nation-state not just because Muslims and non-Muslims live side-by-side in peace and prosperity, but because many Singaporeans deeply believe that our diversity does not divide us and instead is a source of strength.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We believe that Singapore can flourish as a cohesive society and as one united people only if we safeguard the common space for people of all races and religions, including those who do not profess one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: While religion is a deeply personal matter, the community recognises the need for laws as an important enabler to allow communities of different faiths to co-exist in harmony.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The law sets the tone for the norms that we treasure and uphold as a society and, in the case of MRHA, the laws are the ultimate safeguard for religious harmony.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The amendments proposed in this Bill are aligned with our approach of managing Muslim affairs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our Muslim community is a confident one and how we practise our faith is founded on the strong underpinnings of Islam and contextualised to our way of life in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It cannot and should not be influenced by foreign forces, as our community must chart our own way forward, based on the set of values that have allowed Singapore and Singaporeans to thrive in an increasingly polarised world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In support of the launch of the Commitment to Safeguard Religious Harmony in June 2019, Mufti Ustaz Mohamed Fatris Bakaram had said that the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore's (MUIS’) efforts have always been guided by the vision of establishing a common space and advancing the common good for all in our society, and to keep out divisive and isolationist tendencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We can and must continue to be self-reliant so that, as a Singapore Muslim community, we are able to address our own needs without becoming susceptible to manipulation by foreign parties for their own agendas and risking the peace and harmony we have enjoyed as a society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We will not condone any foreign preacher advocating violence, segregationist or intolerant teachings that could divide our multiracial, multi-religious society, and build up unhappiness across different faith communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our community leaders and those of other faiths met with him.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Before leaving Singapore, he apologised, and showed that he understood the implications of his remarks on trust among communities in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Both the Muslim community and non-Muslim Singaporeans welcomed his apology and gesture of reconciliation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: However, we need more than MRHA laws to ensure that our Muslim community remains strongly grounded in how Islam is practised in Singapore’s multi-religious context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Workers’ Party Member of Parliament, Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap, earlier mentioned about how integration is done in Australia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But here in Singapore, we must determine what works best for our unique multi-religious context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: And our schools are critical common spaces where we nurture a shared identity and a shared experience among our children, regardless of race and religion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our entire community, our religious teachers and our leaders, must continue to be proactive and have the conviction that religious harmony is imperative to the survival and success of Singapore, and then to equip ourselves with the knowledge and skills to live out these values every day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is why, to be registered under the Asatizah Recognition Scheme (ARS), one must possess the necessary qualifications as well as abide by the Asatizah Code of Ethics, which states that religious teachings must not encourage extremism or violence, nor denigrate other faiths, and instead inculcate respect and understanding towards others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ARS was introduced as a voluntary scheme in 2005, and community support, including amongst the asatizahs, has been strong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This was underscored when community and religious leaders asked in 2016 for ARS to be made mandatory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: First, the Asatizah Recognition Board (ARB) comprising senior and respected asatizahs in the community oversees ARS, supported by MUIS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Second, the Board and MUIS take ARS registration seriously, instituting provisional periods of observation and requiring additional interviews as the Board deems necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Third, ARS asatizahs are required to attend regular Continuous Professional Education training programmes, and their suitability as an asatizah is periodically reviewed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Their accreditation will be revoked if they breach ARS standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In summary, ARS is a robust, community-led system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It shows the Singapore Muslim community’s strong sense of ownership and commitment to ensuring that its religious teachers are credible and that their teachings are in line with Singapore’s multi-religious context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: PCICS will enable local asatizahs who have been trained in overseas Islamic institutions to remain anchored to Singapore’s multi-religious context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Under PCICS, they will learn about other religions in Singapore, and through this, appreciate the importance of inter-religious understanding in strengthening social cohesion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In my conversations with the asatizah community as part of COFA’s engagement, I am heartened that they recognise the importance of teaching Islam that is suited to our multi-religious societal context and support the introduction of PCICS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our community’s religious leaders also lead by example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They have a strong tradition of working closely with the leaders of other faiths to strengthen interfaith trust and understanding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For instance, our mosques officials are active members of the IRCCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Several asatizahs have been involved in deepening interfaith dialogue and mutual understanding through the "Ask Me Anything" and the Common Senses for Common Spaces (CSCS) dialogue series promoting interfaith conversations, while others volunteer as docents at the Harmony Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Commitment emphasises the common values across different faiths and sets out how Singaporeans of different faiths should interact with one another in a manner that grows trust and social bonds in our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   We often speak about our country's uniqueness as a multiracial and multi-religious society where all races live in harmony.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: History has shown us that nothing we have achieved today happened by chance and we are aware that the necessary efforts should continue in order to preserve this harmony.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This includes maintaining the good relations among the different races through community activities, providing a safe space for dialogue and discussions of sensitive issues, providing infrastructures, such as schools and housing, where we can live and gain common experiences, and also having laws that can specifically hinder acts that can divide our society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: First, to maintain religious harmony by ensuring that the different religions practise moderation and tolerance, and do not do anything that can create any discomfort with one another.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, with changing times and rapid digital breakthroughs, we need to review the effectiveness of this Act in order to protect the nation's well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For instance, fake news can become viral at an amazing speed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Hate commentaries towards any particular religion can also spread very quickly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With technology, influences beyond our borders can easily reach out and damage the trust within society without us realising it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government must have the ability to manage this quickly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Today, we are debating the amendment of an Act that has not been invoked but holds great significance as a symbol of the nation’s commitment to the preservation of harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am heartened that continued and consistent efforts are being made by the Government to ensure that we guard against acts that could tear at our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The advent and proliferation of technology have made the world a different place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With social media, a lot of information, both positive and negative, can go viral very quickly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a need for appropriate legislation in place to ensure that there is ability to quickly respond to acts that could incite hate and ill-will amongst members in the community and respond to foreign interference that could create distrust and divisions in our people without us even being aware.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would just like to comment on several provisions in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The defences appear to make a distinction between acts that are carried out privately and in the public domain.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that it may be impractical to expect the authorities to police private communications.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Any enforcement of the law for action done within certain confines, may also be seen to infringe on certain human liberties of privacy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A more profound hatred could develop over time, through repeated private discussions and with different groups of people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am, therefore, wondering if we could take a more calibrated approach in practice, when such a situation of a private expression of hate or ill-will that is made known to the authorities occurs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In appropriate circumstances, especially when the hate or ill-will arises out ignorance and could worsen if left unchecked, could recommendations be made for the individual to be referred to a community engagement, akin to the CRI?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This leads me to the second provision I would like to comment on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that this approach is potentially a powerful mechanism to really challenge beliefs and behaviours.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Malay, there is a saying, “Tak kenal, maka tak cinta” which means, “You do not know, so you do not love.” Often, resentment or hatred arises from ignorance and lack of understanding of another’s beliefs and practices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The offer must first be made by the Minister, and the person may choose to enter into this scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I acknowledge that one must be given the choice, as compelling anyone into this process would be counterproductive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, I hope that in the implementation of this legislation, efforts will be made to encourage the application of CRI in most cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Minister Shanmugam said at the recent dialogue organised by One People.Sg (OPSG) and Channel NewsAsia that there is no silver bullet to solving racism, but Singapore has had a fair amount of success over the years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The issues of race and religion are intertwined in this country and we need to continue to take efforts to address them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a management committee member of OPSG, I am happy to note that there have been many platforms put forth by OPSG to allow for discussions and meaningful engagements amongst people from different races and religions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are also various focus group discussions, learning journeys and camps for youths, to name a few, that are targeted towards promoting understanding and embracing the diversity of race and religion in our community.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our Government has been putting in great efforts to strengthen racial and religious harmony in Singapore since we gained Independence.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in view of the speed and reach of online communications, we must do this to minimise potential damage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a Chinese saying, 星星之火可以燎原，that a single spark of fire could burn down an entire grassland.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, a comment, a single sentence or a single paragraph on the Internet could trigger discord among groups of people, leading to violence and destruction within hours.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is far better to err on the side of caution even though we might be criticised for being too strict or too sensitive as the stakes are simply too much for our small nation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This challenge is how the Government could increase surveillance over social media and stop any comment or posting that could sow discord among religious groups, especially from offshore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The scope of this task could be overwhelming due to the sheer volume of online postings.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of the providers may resist or ignore our demands, on the pretext of freedom of expression, even when such expressions include untruths, insults and calls to do harm.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are we able to impose effective restraints and meaningful penalties upon uncooperative companies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, would the law be applied to foreigners who have attempted to infiltrate and impose such provocative expressions from offshore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we maintain a blacklist of such perpetrators which Singaporeans can also access so that institutions and organisations will be mindful and think twice about giving them a platform to share their thoughts or give public talks?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Here in Singapore, we must not allow anyone to attempt to sow mistrust among our racial and religious groups.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nobody is allowed to cross the out-of-bounds (OB) markers using the pretext of freedom of belief and speech.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we should not assume that everyone is clear about the OB markers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
