text: Therefore, public education is very important and it should be complemented with regular reminders.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry will share its plans and measures for public education to continue educating Singaporeans, to strengthen mutual understanding of one another’s faiths and practices as well mutual respect and help.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, more can be done to encourage inter-religious cooperation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, we are already seeing many religious groups coming together to support one another.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, recently, a Buddhist group helps with traffic control for visitors to a mosque.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another example is mosques working with churches and temples to help the needy, regardless of race and religion.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, we have come across neighbours’ disputes arising from different religious and cultural practices, such as the burning of joss paper and even the placement of altars.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is really quite remarkable, considering our small population and land size.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our religious diversity and social stability attest to the success of our policies to treat everyone equally, "regardless of race, language or religion", as stated in our citizens' national pledge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This commitment extends to residents of other nationalities living and working here.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Maintaining peaceful co-existence of people from so many different religious and racial groups and of different nationalities in a densely built-up city is no easy feat.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must never take religious harmony for granted nor let our guard down but continue to work on strengthening our social fabric through constant reviews and adjustments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MRHA has been instrumental in preventing anyone or group from inciting feelings of hostility towards people of different religious groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To ensure that its powers remain effective, we need to revise its coverage to keep up with the times.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The ways of communication have changed significantly, and I view the expansion of the scope of ROs as a necessity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, unfiltered messages can spread through the Internet and social media like wildfire, reaching tens and hundreds of thousands in minutes and hours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Within that time, much damage can be done if ROs do not take immediate effect.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we have seen in incidents in other countries, the harm is not just hurt feelings, but the loss of precious lives, irreparable injuries, destruction of infrastructure and, worse, when people react emotionally and violently, often without checking the basis of what they have heard or read.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We also need to factor in the precious time used up in the process of recognising, verifying and identifying such online threats before issuing the RO.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I want to state my support for the introduction of CRI which is non-mandatory and intended to be rehabilitative and restorative.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that a significant portion of the offenders will benefit from the opportunities to better understand themselves and their religion in the context of our multi-religious Singapore, and the religion or religions they have denigrated, through counselling or participation in activities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am hopeful that ties can be mended.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While these individuals are going through CRI, they may not be able to earn a living or take care of their families as usual.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would there be help provided for their family members, such as counselling on financial and household management and even religious guidance, similar to assistance for families of the incarcerated?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am particularly worried about how the elderly and children in affected families will be impacted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appeal to the Ministry to ensure that they will not go hungry and the children will also get to continue their schooling uninterrupted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This may also be a good time to identify how much influence the offenders' beliefs have on their family members, so that they can be similarly assisted and led away from misguided beliefs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the Ministry's assessment of this scenario and the consequences of the offenders being let off, in a way, without penalties?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry share some of the guidelines which inform such exemptions?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern is that too much discretion will be given to the officers in charge and evaluation standards may be uneven.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another safeguard is the requirement to disclose affiliations to foreign organisations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of the smaller religious bodies rely on volunteers and have very lean resources to draw upon.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I seek the Ministry's assurance that the demands of the disclosure are not too onerous.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, would the Ministry elaborate on how to facilitate whistleblowing so that the authorities can pick up news and information of individuals or religious leaders fanning the flames of ill-will and hatred towards targeted groups as early as possible?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On one hand, we want to deter unwarranted complaints or prank calls; on the other hand, the screening process should not be too onerous and discourage genuine reports.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We also need to provide protection for whistleblowers and ensure anonymity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I want to ask about efforts to ensure the spread of public education on basic religious knowledge which is suitable for our multi-religious nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is very important that citizens and residents here at least attain a basic level of discernment and knowledge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Add these to mutual respect, tolerance and a gracious attitude, we will be able to enjoy the fruits of a harmonious and vibrant society for years to come.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   (In Mandarin): Lastly, I want to ask about efforts to ensure the spread of public education on basic religious knowledge which is suitable for our multi-religious nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most people will not actively seek out general knowledge about other religions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: All the world's great religions have a presence in Singapore – Christians, Buddhists, Taoists, Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Sikhs, Baha'is, Jews and Zoroastrians.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a consequence of Singapore from the time of historic Temasek having been a Faith-Hub for leaders and missionaries of all the major religions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, being a faith-hub also brings its own set of challenges.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: To deal with these challenges, in 1990, we enacted MRHA.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: After almost 30 years, these two principles remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments are timely, well-calibrated and much needed in the face of technological disruptions and global threats to uphold peace, security and even sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I wish to speak on three areas – issuance of ROs, CRI and foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, it was fitting that Facebook's founder and Chief Executive, Mark Zuckerburg, had earlier this year said that there was a need for governments and regulators to have "a more active role” on how the social media and Internet are regulated." With the Internet and social media, quicker actions need to be taken to prevent statements which are offensive to religious communities from spreading here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Social media is akin to forest fires, where a lit matchstick on a beautiful summer day can cause a massive wildfire.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: A single offensive or thoughtless post by such figures can be seen by millions within a few hours, thus creating a tense situation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: How can we safeguard Singaporeans from having access to such content on social platforms given the introduction of the extraterritoriality clause in this amendment Bill?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The revised process of Issuance of ROs is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In keeping with the ethos of MRHA not being a punitive act, the CRI is a welcome addition.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen CRI in action on a few notable occasions in Singapore in recent times.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In 2017, an Imam of a mosque who had made controversial remarks about Christians and Jews apologised for his actions to a group of faith leaders.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In 2018, a Pastor apologised to Muslim leaders for a guest US preacher’s hurtful statements on Islam.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: More recently, last month, as quoted by the Minister, a social media influencer apologised for an insensitive remark about two Sikh gentlemen’s headgears at the Formula One Grand Prix and subsequently joined and took part in the community outreach efforts of the Sikh community.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In all three incidents above, the apologies rendered and subsequent interactions with the faith leaders and communities concerned were restorative, rehabilitative and, I would say, reconciliatory in nature.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: CRI was a reality without a name in all three incidents.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For those who genuinely, without malice, cross the religious harmony line, CRI offers a fair and balanced means to set right what was made wrong.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, on foreign influence, the term "foreign influence" need not connote a negative meaning completely.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The IRO in Singapore is a living example of what constructive foreign influence can do for a multi-religious environment like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In 1949, Maulana Muhammad Abdul Aleem Siddiqui, known as the 20th century’s roving ambassador of Islam, landed on our shores to great acclaim to deliver a message of peace.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Representatives of the major religions were catalysed and met again in a series of two further meetings and it culminated in the formation of the body known as the IRO which marked its 70th anniversary just this year.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is very fortunate that our founding generation laid the foundations for a harmonious and peaceful country, with subsequent generations working hard to strengthen the trust, tolerance and mutual respect among the different faiths.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, the world we live in today is starkly different and is definitely not a bed of roses.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Going back to the second objective which I shared earlier on MRHA, religion and politics must be kept separate.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is simply not the case in today’s context where we find numerous nefarious examples of religion being used to advance political causes.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We are witnessing many of these on our television screens every passing day and we must never allow religion to be weaponised in Singapore, or to be used as a front for other conflicts.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially so in the case of "goodwill donations" and "cash gifts" that are presented when a prayer is answered, or a vow is fulfilled or simply to seek the blessings of a guru or deity.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: They shared that they may not have adequate resources to dedicate for this disclosure purpose.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Ministry view and act in such cases?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The possibility of manipulation by foreign agents is very real, and religious organisations should view these amendments positively to protect their congregations and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, no one likes controls, but it is inevitable to maintain harmony.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For the larger common good, these are necessary.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):   Religious Harmony is a uniquely Singaporean effort.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: While many of us may disregard this, we must remember that, in Singapore, we have made a concerted effort over many generations to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This did not happen by chance; many years of forging friendships, fostering understanding, building mutual trust, and creating legislative structures, Singapore is an inevitable "Faith-hub" today.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments in this Bill should ensure religious harmony in our society, not just for the next 30 years but for many more years beyond.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a testament to the will and courage of our religious, community and political leaders, both past and present.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, for these reasons of meeting today's challenges and needs that I stand in support of the amendments to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, we have never had the need to use the Act in almost three decades of its existence.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I pray that the amendments will be deterrent enough to warrant many more years of the Act not being used.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans often proudly cite the fact that Singapore is a country where many religions can co-exist peacefully and even thrive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot take this state of affairs for granted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is an acknowledgment that we must constantly update our legal framework to address new challenges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The most pressing ones we face right now are the challenges posed by social media and the Internet, as well as the trend of foreign influence exploiting religious fault lines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has closely consulted religious leaders in drafting the Bill and I understand that there is strong support from religious leaders for these amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened to see that while the challenges have evolved, the Government’s consultative relationship with religious leaders and groups when it comes to religious matters has not changed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, citizenship or permanent residence is a very rough proxy for whether an individual is under foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just this year alone, two Singaporean men were detained in January, while another two were detained in May and July.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All four men had been radicalised by pro-Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) elements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They were Singapore Citizens but acting under the influence of foreign actors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How does this Bill propose to address foreign influence on religious organisations where the influence does not come directly from foreign actors, but from citizens or PRs who are acting under foreign influence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 8(2A) specifies the reasons for which an RO may be made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On what grounds under section 8(2A) can an RO be made to address foreign influence exerted through Singapore Citizens in a religious organisation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But with so many exemptions proposed, my concern is whether this requirement will be effective.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are exempting "foreigners in Singapore on long-term passes".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is probably more justifiable to exempt Singapore Citizens and Singapore PRs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But since the amendment is proposed to safeguard against foreign influence, can the Minister clarify why the exemption is extended to "foreigners in Singapore on long-term passes"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The exemption is also for anonymous donations like those made via donation boxes placed at the religious sites.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This exemption seems quite straightforward since we do not know who made those donations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, how will we prevent people from exploiting this loophole?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A foreigner could inform a religious organisation that he or she is making a donation of $10,000 or more but, to circumvent the need to disclose this donation to the authorities, he or she will drop the donation in the donation box.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He or she could also ask a foreigner in Singapore on a long-term pass to help make that donation but still alert the religious organisation that the donation is from him or her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suggest that we also require religious organisations to disclose any correspondence with foreigners with regard to donations of large amounts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This can be similar to the proposed requirement for religious organisations to disclose affiliations to foreign individuals or organisations which are in a position of control or power over the religious organisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can I also ask if the Ministry is tracking how much foreign donations a religious organisation is receiving annually and also how much it is receiving anonymously?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There might be cases where a religious organisation which receives a significant amount of foreign donations but does not need to disclose their foreign donations as it is from different sources and each source of donation is under $10,000.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do believe that we should monitor this, be alert, and pay attention to religious organisations which have significant amounts of or have sudden increases in foreign donation which do not need to be disclosed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This should apply also to sudden increases in anonymous donations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond these suggestions, can the Minister provide more assurances that the exemptions proposed will not become loopholes, which makes it harder to safeguard against foreign influence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CRI has a similar objective as a Community Service Order (CSO), which is a sentence that can be imposed for an offender to make amends to the community by performing unpaid community service under the supervision of an authorised officer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The difference between CRI and a CSO is that the decision to offer the CRI is made by the Minister, making it different from a CSO, which is a punishment imposed by a judge.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CRI is intended to be offered at the pre-trial stage, as opposed to a CSO which features at the post-trial, sentencing stage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, both CRI and a CSO have similar underlying rationales of rehabilitation and education.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The need to rehabilitate and re-educate an offender is still present even after an offender has been tried.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, beyond MRHA or the proposed amendments, what is even more remarkable is the collaborative relationship between the Government and our religious organisations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The religious groups have a close relationship based on mutual trust and respect, and frequently interact through platforms, such as the IROs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The success of our multi-religious society lies not just with our laws but also our approach in managing inter-religious relations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our focus will continue to remain on education and building inter-religious ties, and that we will never have to resort to the mechanisms under MRHA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The late Dr Ong Chit Chung, former Member of Parliament for Bukit Batok and my predecessor, stated presciently in this House at the Third Reading of the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Bill on 9 November 1990, and I quote, "This Bill is a preventive measure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It need not be used at all if all is well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But its very presence will help to check mischievous or misguided persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the aims of the Bill in principle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that it also has broad support of the local religious leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim has some reservations that the religious leaders made statements to this effect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The suggestion, I believe, she made is that by making such statements, they may have crossed the religion-political divide.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These statements, as I recall, were issued after MHA actively sought the leaders’ views.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a responsible thing to do because a number of the provisions in this Bill are focused on religious leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, the Select Committee in 1990 also benefited from the views of the religious leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It should be borne in mind that the religious leaders consulted, whether they supported the Bill, was not, pardon the pun, preordained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As it turned out, after the consultative process and after their views had been taken into account into the Bill is presented in this House, they gave their support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, the leaders’ expression of support, or for that matter, even if they have expressed reservation or dissent to the Bill in these circumstances, does not, in my respectful view, equate to mixing religion with politics.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have three points to make on the Bill proper and one query on the proposed powers for the Minister to make subsidiary legislation under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A number of hon Members spoke about this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I join Ms Anthea Ong in making the point that the focus of the removal of the 14-day period appears to be because of the fact that you have such statements being made on the Internet and there could be a viralling effect very quickly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the wording of the provision applies broadly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, in those circumstances, I wonder whether the rationale behind this provision in the first place that has been identified by the Select Committee as the safeguard, which is through requiring the Minister to take notice of the individual’s representation before proceeding further, can be adopted for situations which do not involve the Internet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And what is not clear is that, at this point in time, whether the Ministry could say that, most likely, all the situations, or most of the situations, we are dealing with representations or statements made through the Internet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That part is not clear, and I would be grateful for the hon Minister’s views on this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I move on to the proposed section 16H which deals with CRI, and many Members spoke positively about this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is meant to rehabilitate the person in question and to promote reconciliation with the wounded community and victims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister’s reference to the laudable initiative by the Young Sikhs Association inviting a blogger, who made a statement which can be seen as offensive, to a Sikh gurdwara with a view to rehabilitate her is an excellent example of how the CRI can work in future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The starting point, however, is that the person in question is believed to have committed offences of causing ill-will between different groups or wounding religious feelings of any other person.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are offences under Penal Code provisions which are proposed to be ported over to MRHA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I agree with the porting over, but my concern is the interplay between the Attorney-General’s powers and the Minister’s powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, the Minister decides whether or not to offer the CRI, and while the CRI is implemented, there can be no prosecution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, you could have a situation where the Attorney-General may decide to prosecute a person, only not to be able to proceed with the issuance of the CRI by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be better to vest with the Attorney-General this power or at least require the Minister to get the Attorney-General’s consent beforehand?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, in this regard, I declare my interest as a lawyer in private practice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This provision invited much scrutiny in this House when the Bill was debated in 1990.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The decision to oust the jurisdiction of the Court is based on mainly the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A decision to issue an RO is a political decision, not a judicial decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Executive Government is ultimately accountable to our people through the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This compares in stark contrast to judges who are appointed to their post.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There was widespread property damage and fires, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a need to move fast and decisively, and this is something where Court proceedings may not necessarily be an answer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have previously made a suggestion in this House this provision be relooked with a view to allowing Court scrutiny and welcome this opportunity to elaborate on my reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the heart of the issue is to ensure that MRHA will continue to enjoy legitimacy amongst our people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Allowing decisions under MRHA to be judicially reviewed by the Court does not lead to a replacement of a political decision with a judicial one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Any concerns that the Court proceedings which are open to public may inflame tensions can be dealt with procedurally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Most importantly, there is a safeguard against abuse of power in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not enough to say that Executive is still accountable to the public through elections.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The concern I have is to ensure legitimacy of MRHA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not gained just by obtaining the imprimatur of the majority who voted in the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also important to deal with minority interests.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is to ensure that all segments of our society are united.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Lord Sumption, a retired UK Law Lord, pithily put this point across extrajudicially in the 2019 Reith Lectures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, "Majority rule is the basic principle of democracy, but that only means that a majority is enough to authorise the State’s acts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is because majority rule is no more than a rule of decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It does nothing to accommodate our differences, it simply restates them in numerical terms."   One good example of taking care of the minority interests is the Presidential Council of Minority Rights (PCMR) articles in the Constitution dealing with Acts that may discriminate against minorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that was raised by the Prime Minister when he was Deputy Prime Minister during the Second Reading of MRHA in the House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our Courts should be allowed to act as a safeguard against abuse of power against individuals in future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members of the public are not necessarily in a good position to parse through evidence and draw the necessary conclusions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Judges, on the other hand, have the skill and ability and they are also highly regarded as an independent pillar in our Westminster-style Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The point I make is not new, as the hon Member, Mr Pritam Singh noted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister himself made the same points at the Second Reading of the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Bill in 1990.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I stress, my concern is ensuring that for the next 30 years and beyond, the MRHA provisions will continue to enjoy legitimacy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister spoke about the rise in identity politics in the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is something which may catch root even in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And having judicial oversight would help keep our community together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The way it reads is that it is proposed that the Minister create these offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or in any event, what are the offences that are being proposed?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Deputy Speaker, this review of MRHA is a timely move.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Growing connectivity, be it the widespread proliferation of social media or convenient travel across physical borders, has allowed religious organisations and followers around the world to reach out to one another.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And with our nation located at the crossroads of this region, it is increasingly common for religious leaders to travel to Singapore to conduct seminars.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this age of the Internet, their books, for example, are readily available online.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some have made their way into local bookstores.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some speakers may even make use of social media to broadcast their seminars via Youtube and other platforms without stepping foot in Singapore, and believers can learn from them in the comfort of their own homes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For those who have religious beliefs, religion gives one guidance and comfort when one is going through a bad patch in one’s life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As Singapore is a cosmopolitan city with people from around the world taking up permanent or semi-permanent residency, it is important that their religions remain accessible to them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mutual respect and understanding of various religious practices have allowed Singapore to remain a safe, stable and prosperous nation, and this must continue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was demonstrated, for instance, in Toa Payoh East-Novena recently, when non-Malay/Muslim volunteers jointly helped to pay for the airfare costs of a Malay/Muslim grandmother whose grandson was fatally shot by extremists in Christchurch.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nevertheless, I note that there are some people who teach religion or preach in the privacy of their own domains, such as at home, private halls and so forth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are not open to the public, and only people who have been invited are allowed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These mostly consist of their own circle of friends, who would then, through word of mouth, invite their own friends and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is common among non-Singaporeans or foreigners who may prefer a group that shares their nationality and language, but it also happens among some locals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some are splinter groups with a small following; perhaps they could not agree with the mainstream ideologies of their religion, so they decided to improvise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, the topic may not have any religious connotation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, it could have an innocuous title like “Challenges we face in our life”, for example, and the speaker can then weave in religious ideas and so forth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Then there are cases of religious teachers who are self-proclaimed religious experts, who approach individual places of worship, get a small audience of people, preach, collect a donation, then disappear.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or if they are foreigners or non-Singapore Citizens, they may leave the country.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sometimes, they do not lecture, but they may screen a video.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister clarify if this constitutes as a definition of preaching?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, it would likely boil down to one of the attendees to tip-off the Police or their loved ones to realise that something is amiss and make a Police report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The recent case of domestic helpers who were radicalised is, indeed, an eye-opener.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must remember that radicalisation can affect anyone, man and woman, young and old, and from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do employers look out for such cases?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, domestic helpers have their days off and are able to go out and mix freely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the local organisation have to delink itself?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would like to ask what if a speaker is from a diplomatic mission?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If he addresses an audience on religious matters, would he be governed under this law or is he exempted because of his diplomatic status?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I applaud the Government’s determination to prevent the spread of offensive statements against any religious group.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think it could also happen the other way around when a religious group unintentionally offends another religious group or group of people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And there are words, for example, like “heathen” or “pagan” or “infidels”, or “idolater” which can inflame feelings and be regarded as offensive under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could Minister offer some guide on the usage of such words in terms of their definition and their use within this Act?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many offensive and insensitive acts to other religions or races occur due to lack of awareness rather than out of hatred.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note one recent incident that was already highlighted by several Members in this Chamber where a social media influencer offended members of the Sikh community with her controversial remarks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Young Sikh Association reached out to her and invited her to the Central Sikh Temple so they could share more about their religion with her.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She even got to participate in some of their activities, and it was a good learning experience for everyone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a great example of a remedial initiative to educate the offender.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we need to be mindful of the aspects which could pose challenges to religious harmony in our society.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: New citizens and foreigners may not be familiar with living in a multicultural and multi-religious environment and there may be more diversity in the practice of faith, which can cause potential rifts and conflict among practitioners.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While I was going through the Bill, I thought of Muhammed Haniff Abdul Razak, my long-time family friend, who has devoted a big part of his life to inter- and intra-faith harmony work.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Haniff was previously serving on the Islamic Religious Council in Singapore and was tasked by MUIS President Encik Alami Musa to set up a Harmony Centre in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Together with Imam Habib Hassan and Ms Hairani Hassan, they came together to devise a concept and pioneered this initiative that provides inter-faith services in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This Singaporean concept of a Harmony Centre has deeply impressed many interfaith organisations across the world.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: And, with that, in 2010, Haniff was invited by the esteemed Prof Venerable Master Chin Kung and the Late Mr Ng Kim Suan to set up a similar centre in Australia, and since then, shared and replicated this model with many other countries, such as the UK, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and many others.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This clearly demonstrates how our little red dot can be an incubator for innovative models and influencing practices all across the world.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I was introduced to several religious leaders, educators and interfaith advocates through Haniff and while most of them are generally supportive of this Bill's amendments, they do have some concerns that they have laid out in the hope that the Government will consider them.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: We must place trust in our respected and learned religious leaders to be accountable, and reduce the administrative burden on these organisations.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Some religious leaders are concerned that this requirement will add on more administrative work and may deter future donations needed to support their community work, as some donors may prefer to remain anonymous.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As there are many ways for external influence to act on a country and disrupt societal harmony, would it not be possible to deal with these concerns as a whole through a Foreign Interference or Social Harmony Act?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This way, if practices are breached, regardless of whether they are religious in nature or not, they can be dealt with similarly, instead of incorporating into this Bill and putting an unflattering spotlight on religion.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: All religious societies in Singapore have their origins overseas and it is not uncommon that their leaders are appointed from their head organisations overseas.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that MHA do have provisions for exemptions on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Can it provide assurance that this change will not compromise their leadership appointment process?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: MHA has been very vigilant in monitoring religious matters happening in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: We all know the stakes are very high when it comes to maintaining racial and religious harmony and any imbalance can severely affect security, peace and stability.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: We can do more to strengthen community cohesion and engagement through forming a conclave of renowned, highly respectable community leaders, and empower them as spokesmen to front religious sensitive matters.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Such an initiative is apparent to MUIS, but more can be done to extend this to other religious organisations.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This can help to promote community ownership for sensitive matters related to religion.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: A select group of official, religious mediators can also support these leaders through mediation and cross religion practice awareness training, also coordinated and assisted by MHA.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to posit a case where religious sensitivity was involved.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: An elderly Muslim man lived alone and was neglected by his family.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: To stave off loneliness, he joined a Church, participated in Christian activities and, over the years, decided to embrace Christianity.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, he became very ill and one of his last wishes was to die as a Christian and be buried according to Christian rites.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Subsequently, the family came to know of this and made a Court injunction to stop him from being buried with Christian rites.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The Church countered this challenge and brought the matter to Court.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For such a scenario, religious mediators are much needed by the authorities to step in and find an amicable solution.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Greater emphasis should also be placed on intra-faith harmony.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While the IRO Council promotes interfaith harmony, it is equally important for us to focus on intra-faith harmony.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There are many examples of intra-faith conflicts all around the world for us to learn from, such as the Shia-Sunni conflict in the Middle East.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, it is important for us to follow the principle of "every Singaporean matters".

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I also understand that the National Steering Committee (NSC) on Racial and Religious Harmony is a national platform built to bring together top levels of community, the Government and faith leaders.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This prevents citizens from having a stronger understanding of each religion so that they feel comfortable and safe to engage in discussion.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: A successful, harmonious society should be one where we understand one another’s religion and are able to openly share without causing tension, rather than one where people choose to be silent and harbour ignorant ideals of another’s religion.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I quote Prime Minister Lee’s recent speech in New York that "Singapore is ranked the most religiously diverse country in the world, but its harmonious society did not come about by chance." His words remind me of the numerous unsung heroes in Singapore, committed to their vital roles to bring peace and harmony to our country.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: They include our inter-Ministerial colleagues, our Home Team, religious leaders, interfaith advocates, responsible media and a strong Singaporean community.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to MHA’s response to my proposals and the concerns raised by some of our religious leaders.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The maintenance of religious harmony, the upkeep of and the elimination of any threat to public peace and public order, are paramount to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must do all we can to preserve the religious harmony that is critical for the survivability of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I fully support the amendments in this Bill which are aimed at maintaining this harmony.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are some areas of the Bill to which I seek clarification.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Before I seek my clarifications, please allow me to speak in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   We all fundamentally agree that it is important for Singapore to maintain racial harmony.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This peaceful and harmonious environment is created by establishing trust among the different races and religions that was imbued since Independence by many of our community leaders, including our accredited asatizahs, as well as our other community leaders.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the racial harmony that we enjoy can become fragile and easily destroyed if we are not careful and vigilant in maintaining the strong bonds that exist among us.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must recognise and admit that there are certain groups that want to unravel or destroy the bonds of trust among the different races and religions in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Religious beliefs and ethnicity are matters that are close to the hearts of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singaporeans, we can practise our own religions peacefully and undisturbed by anyone.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This situation did not exist by chance and must be looked after judiciously and wisely.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I welcome MHA’s move to propose amendments to this Act in order to further strengthen the laws that safeguard racial and religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): As mentioned earlier, Mr Deputy Speaker, there are some areas of the Bill in which I seek clarifications.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, there may be a donor who is known to a person or persons in a religious organisation, but who decides to give an “anonymous donation” by dropping in a sum of money to a donation box of the organisation, and where the act and purpose of the donation has been made known to the organisation.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this case, in terms of audit and accounting, the donor is anonymous.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But in reality, the donor is known to someone in the organisation and the act and purpose of the donation is also known.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this case, how can the proper KYD be carried out?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the donation be returned to the donor?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will interactions and communication between the donor and known person or persons in the organisation be more closely scrutinised?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there ways in which the Minister can exercise his power to obtain further information about the donor?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To what extent does the Minister seek the counsel of this “competent authority” on matters pertaining to ROs?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will this “competent authority” be someone from PCRH?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Both our diversity and social cohesion are equally precious and important to us, and it is imperative that both are upheld and protected.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am confident the amendments in this Bill will help to further strengthen our social cohesion, provide greater protection to our religious and racial harmony, and ensure public peace and order in our society.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is multi-religious and multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: For many years, Singaporeans have witnessed different races and religions co-existing harmoniously, but we cannot take it for granted.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: As time changes, ill-intended radicals can make use of the various new media to create xenophobia, and extremist groups will even stage terror attacks to stir up social unrest.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: What is unsettling is that terrorism is also threatening Singapore.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is aware of this worrying trend and has taken more measures to prevent the problem from getting worse.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I agree that MRHA must be kept up to date to safeguard Singapore's religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We must work together to maintain and strengthen our religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We have also set up the IRCCs to strengthen social cohesion and expand our contact network.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: MCCY set up SGSecure Community Network two years ago to support the SGSecure movement, helping IRCCs grassroots' work.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, Singapore's different races and religions have been living peacefully together.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They have always been accommodating, which sets a key tone for social stability.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the Singapore Buddhist Federation seeks to promote cultural education and groom the future generation.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They also founded schools, childcare centres and Buddhist youth groups.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Through its bursary awards, the Federation provides various social services to needy students from different races.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The Federation spares no effort in promoting religious harmony and plays an important role in maintaining Singapore's racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: These activities help to strengthen bonding amongst Singaporeans and build a common identity.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The Al-Istighfar Mosque at Pasir Ris provides guided tours to non-Muslims and introduced an initiative called "Water For All" to benefit different races and religions, and to deepen the understanding among one another.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) organises many local and overseas community services.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The volunteers have made an impact on all members of the community, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I recommend that the Government include Culture Studies in our education curriculum.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: To respect and understand one another is the foundation of a united Singapore, especially because we are a multiracial, multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Integrating Culture Studies into students' curriculum will allow students to study the similarities and the differences between different cultures, providing a platform for different races to interact with one another.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Just like Social Studies lessons in school, I think Culture Studies will help Singaporeans to better understand a particular culture and better communicate with people from other races.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: These lessons can be thought provoking as well, inspiring us to learn from one another.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They can make us more considerate and understanding.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: When we interact with people from other religions, we should accommodate one another.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The friendship and understanding among our different races in Singapore are not formed overnight.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, mutual trust and good relations are built over years through common experiences and interactions.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: These valuable social assets must be passed down to the future generations.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Religious leaders, community leaders and Singaporeans must work together to build a united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The implementation of Culture Studies can aid this process.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This goes in line with our pledge: We, the citizens of Singapore, Pledge ourselves as one united people, Regardless of race, language or religion, To build a democratic society based on justice and equality, So as to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, Sir, Singapore is a multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: As Singaporeans, we observe that followers of different religions exercise understanding and tolerance.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: MRHA is the law that was enacted in 1990 to help authorities prevent friction and misunderstanding among religious groups.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: However, with the proliferation of social media, one with ill intention may use it to divide Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we need to keep this law up to date and I am in support of this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: However, beyond supporting, I believe there are more can be done.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Strengthening our social cohesion is a shared responsibility for all races and religions.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone plays a part to safeguard our way of life and keep one another safe.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The IRCCs are interfaith platforms in every constituency, formed to promote racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The work of IRCCs is instrumental in strengthening our social cohesion and supports the SGSecure movement.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: At present, the IRCCs deepen people's understanding of the various faiths, beliefs and practices through interfaith and inter-ethnic themed activities, such as heritage trails, interfaith talks and various ethnic and religious celebrations.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Throughout these years, all races and religions live harmoniously together, with understanding and respect for one another.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the Singapore Buddhist Federation (SBF) seeks to promote culture, education and social welfare.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They, too, help to groom the future generation and founded schools, childcare centres, youth groups and so on.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: YMCA organises many local and overseas community services.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The volunteers served and impacted all members of the community, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The study of culture and heritage, cultural elements of each race and religion allows Singaporeans to learn, understand and appreciate the different groups.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: These thought-provoking lessons aim to enhance understanding, as well as empathy.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, the friendship and tacit understanding of different ethnic groups in our country did not happen overnight.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They are fundamentally based on accumulated experiences, interactions and understanding and are built on mutual trust and good relations.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: And this valuable social asset must continue and get passed down to the future generations.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The implementation of culture studies classes, through concerted efforts, will also aid in maintaining peace and harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I rise in support of the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As both an employer and a representative of the Singapore business community, there is no doubt that the religious harmony that we now enjoy in Singapore should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As Prime Minister Lee noted in his recent address in New York, our approach is "strictly secular, but not anti-religious".

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: That many religions are able to co-exist harmoniously in our small island-nation brings valuable diversity to our economy.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, employers having peace of mind for a stable and reliable workforce reaps significant intangible benefits.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: By the same coin, employees can take heart in planning their careers knowing that they are not discriminated against by virtue of their religion.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Our Singapore today is a uniquely Singaporean society where all religions are accorded respect.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Race and religion are both personally sensitive matters and are held close to the heart by our people.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The 1964 racial riots where violent clashes between communities of different races demonstrated how intolerance and a lack of understanding can lead to detrimental results.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Since Independence, a number of social constructs were implemented to encourage inclusion and to foster deeper relations among racial and religious groups within the community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This approach has yielded fruit over the years and I believe all Singaporeans have memories visiting homes of friends of different races and religions during the different festivals and occasions in a year.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: These are activities that are commonplace for us and are easily taken for granted in today’s society.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, it is important that we and the younger generation do not forget that this state of harmony definitely did not happen by accident, but rather by foresight by our leaders in the formative years of our nation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is then our responsibility to continue to do our best to ensure we protect this harmony that is uniquely Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments proposed in the Bill are, therefore, timely.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by MHA, much has changed in the way society communicates since the Bill first came into force in 1992.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While, as widely reported in the media, the provisions in the current Act have never been invoked, we cannot afford to leave things to chance and not reflect changing times and practice.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Our people must continue to know and understand that any such freedoms must always be preceded by responsibility.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on to my second point, I applaud the efforts of the amendments for the more moderate stance it takes towards offenders.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Offenders are not immediately sent to Court, but rather, are encouraged to undergo CRI where they are given an opportunity to reconcile their religious differences.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This reflects the sensitive approach that the Ministry has taken and sets a tone for collaboration and continued education for society.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, it must also be equally important for such an individual to be reintegrated into our Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Continued support for the individual's rehabilitation and education must be available.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, appeal to the Ministry to continue its good work and to extend all such necessary support as required.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Religious organisations now, to some extent, are more complex than they were in the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I believe it is prudent for religious organisations to have more accountability as proposed by the amendments to the Act.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Similar to heads of companies, leaders of religious organisations, indeed, need to be held to a higher standard of behaviour.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: To date, our leaders of religious organisations have been strongly committed to the religious harmony of Singapore, and we must take steps to protect this harmony, borne out of respect and humility.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This coincides with the 70th Anniversary of IRO.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is testament to the sheer amount of work that goes into creating a united society of multiple religions.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by Prime Minister Lee, "This year, our religious leaders made a formal collective declaration that it is entirely proper, and indeed praiseworthy, for people of different faiths to befriend each other, exchange felicitations on each other's religious festivals and eat together despite different dietary rules." Negative foreign influence cannot be allowed to impugn on the intricately woven fabric of our Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is a society which has been nurtured to be religiously tolerant, providing for a stable country and a safe home.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: A happy employee and a happy employer translate to greater efficiency and focus on business needs and, therefore, a happy Government.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This simplification of the tripartite partnership conceals the hard work that the partnership puts in to encourage dialogue and keep open channels of communication.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Religion is an important part of many people's lives and, in Singapore, people of different religious groups have no trouble living harmoniously together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my family, my father's family is Hindu, my mother's family is Christian, my wife is Buddhist and my mother-in-law is Catholic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I myself am not religious, but we have no trouble at all coming together as an extended family in different ways celebrating different occasions together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I grew up with copies of the Bible, Koran, Bhagvad Gita and the teachings of Buddha, all on the same bookshelf.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When I go to a religious house of worship, I am always interested in finding out more about the practices, about the religion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And, to me, it is a way of developing learning.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My life is, in some way, a microcosm of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Admiralty, I say we are very blessed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have a mosque, the Yusof Ishak Mosque, a Buddhist monastery, the BW Monastery and a church, Covenant Evangelical Free Church.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Through the IRCC, all three come together regularly and work together on initiatives, including dialogue sessions, "harmony walks" and regularly support one another's community efforts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In true Singapore spirit, they not only practise tolerance, but also understanding and warmth for one another.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But if one looks at human history, disputes along religious lines are almost as old as time itself, and what we have in Singapore is actually quite exceptional and not an accident.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We just look at some of the festering disputes in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Palestine, for example, the differences between Christians, Muslims and Jews have made resolution of the dispute very difficult.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The holy city of Jerusalem is holy to all three and there is no simple answer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The tensions between Saudi Arabia and Iran also divide along the old lines between the Shi'ites and the Sunnis.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And, again, there is no easy resolution there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The civil war in Ireland between the North and South, also divided along Protestant and Catholic lines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Sri Lanka, there was a historical dispute between the Tamils and the Sinhalese, involving not only differences along language and race but also along religion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is simplistic to see language as the cause of these disputes; but religion was definitely a factor that made them more difficult to resolve.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even developed countries which do not have a history of violence are not immune to foreign disputes spilling over.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Throughout the last few years, ISIS has been spreading terror virally through the Internet as well as through organisations, and attacks have taken place in Paris and London and other capitals with people claiming allegiance to ISIS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In March this year, in New Zealand, a country which has almost no history of religious violence, a shooting took place in a mosque during Friday prayers, killing dozens of people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In April, a month later, there was a series of coordinated attacks in Sri Lanka on Easter, again a country with no history of violence against the Christians, but in this particular case, inspired by foreign disputes, killing more than 250 people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was one of the worst attacks on a Christian community in Asia in recent history.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Later that month, in a Synagogue in San Francisco, there was another attack, this time, by a shooter claiming he was taking revenge.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These attacks are happening in developed countries, all being attributed to religion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Religious violence is clearly growing in different places, and Singapore should not be complacent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We had some of our people taken under ISA for being self-radicalised.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this includes control over donations and people who may take leadership positions in the religious groups.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is all entirely fair and it is not rigid because if any group wishes special consideration, they may apply to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This strikes a right balance that deviations from the requirements of foreign leadership must be exceptional.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The tools available to the Ministry also include tools to pre-empt trouble and not just respond to it once it has happened.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes the use of ROs to restrict what may be said or published or to restrict donations coming in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: More broadly, section 16G allows the competent authority to request information from any religious group to investigate whether there has been compliance by that religious group.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are all calibrated tools that allow the Ministry to come in before trouble has taken place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, offences also include offences by corporations and unincorporated associations, but also provide for individuals within these organisations to be individually responsible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This places the balance fairly and holds organisations and individuals responsible for their actions in line with their culpability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In my speech, Members will see that I use the phrases "wisdom", "care", "sensibility", "practicality" a number of times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That would be, in essence, what I would say to many of the questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let me start by saying I am heartened by the support of the Bill by everyone who spoke.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some questions, but everyone believes that this should be done and that this is the correct thing to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let me now try and address the points raised by the Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been a lot of points by a lot of Members so I hope I can cover them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Alex Yam asked whether there were any concerns, such as those raised in the White Paper in 1990 which required these proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members agree that our religious organisations need safeguards against foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay asked whether there should be an omnibus legislation on foreign influence, instead of including these safeguards in MRHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Members recognise that legislation is needed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a matter of where these laws need to be sited.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about whether leadership requirements will cover corporatised religious charitable groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The outcomes we want, that is, that organisations that propagate, teach and practise religion should be subject to the principles which are set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those principles apply, regardless of whether the organisations are societies or companies limited by guarantees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it does not cover organisations that may have a religious background but do not have as their purpose the promotion of any religious worship or religion, or whose business does not concern religious affairs or practices or conducting, teaching or propagating any religious belief.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Act has been applied for a long time in a sensible way and we will continue to do this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are religious organisations that set up companies to do commercial trading.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think those companies will necessarily be affected, but we have to look at what they are doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Irene Quay expressed concern that the requirements may be too onerous.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Alex Yam requested that MHA engage with religious organisations to clarify these requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also asked about the feedback that has been received.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had discussions with various religious organisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also engaged non-apex religious organisations – the larger temples and all the Catholic Orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We made some changes along the way, based on their feedback.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The religious organisations know there will be some additional work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But they understood and accepted the rationale and the need for these safeguards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been working with them for more than a year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay asked how we set the threshold at $10,000 and how this compares with money laundering and counterterrorism legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Money laundering thresholds take reference from standards set by the Financial Action Task Force.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For terrorism financing, likewise, action is taken however small the amount.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have taken action against persons for $60.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, those actions are in a different league and are extremely strict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For MRHA, we discussed with the apex religious organisations on what an appropriate level would be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to balance between the risk and also the effort that religious organisations have to take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you set it at too low an amount, they will have to take a lot of effort and it may not be meaningful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay asked about examples of past cases where foreign donations have been used to influence local religious organisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am unable to give those examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members go back and, for those who know that we did these things, the first-generation leaders put in some practices that I must say had amazing foresight, and I say this with hindsight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
