text: Because in the last 30 years, what you have seen is that all over the world, money from the Middle East has been used to fund mosques and religious institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The result is that this influences and changes the practice of Islam, which itself has been changed very substantially.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our first-generation leaders put in initiatives, such as the Mosque Building Fund, where local Muslims donate to build our local mosques.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, for the building of mosques, the land is not tendered for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that, effectively, made it very unlikely that foreign funding will come in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have not been affected in the same way as a lot of other countries have been, where money from the Middle East has come in – because that money comes in with tight conditions that the preacher must have been trained in specific countries, and in all likelihood, the preachers would come from those countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And after a while, and now you see it, the entire way in which people practise the religion changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng spoke about the loopholes in the donation requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those examples have elements of deceit – where a foreigner passes off his donation as anonymous or from another person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have offences to deal with donors and religious groups that use fraud, really, to escape disclosure requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we do not want to put too many requirements on these organisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about a foreigner donating $9,999.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, for any threshold we set, someone can donate a dollar less.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we did not set a threshold, then religious organisations will have to track every single donation and that is not feasible either.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we believe that there are influence operations going on, based on intelligence or otherwise, then we can move to an RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why the exemptions for donations disclosure also apply to foreigners on long-term passes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Religious institutions and groups in Singapore serve foreigners as well as locals who stay in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have foreigners who live here, work here, study here, go to local religious institutions, temples, churches and so on, and they naturally donate to them and, again, we did not want to and we do not want to impose too many administrative burdens on our religious organisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about what we can do about citizens or PRs who act as agents of foreign influence in local religious groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will have to look at other legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Alex Yam asked about religious organisations where leadership appointments involve an external decision, due to historical reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are very mindful of that, and we always knew that those are not areas where we can go and direct, require or impose requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And for other organisations as well, exemptions will be granted on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have met many of these organisations and have explained this to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Catholic Church came out in support of the amendments because they understood what we are trying to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay and Ms Joan Pereira sought more details on the criteria for exemptions on leadership requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Without being comprehensive or exclusive, I will say we will consider the following: whether the congregation is largely made up of foreigners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some small religious organisations which serve exclusively a foreign community and, sometimes, it may not be practical to impose on them the requirements that we have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will also look at the structure of the religious organisation and whether it operates as one entity across different countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will also, of course, look at security concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah raised a good suggestion that foreign appointment holders who are granted exemptions, that they should be given basic education on our multi-religious context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about whether local religious organisations would need to delink themselves from "unapproved" overseas organisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MRHA does not provide for powers to ask a local religious organisation to dissociate itself from a foreign affiliate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My colleague Ms Sun Xueling made this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have no homegrown religion of our own and we are an open society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The approach is to ensure that our local religious organisations are sensitised to our multi-religious context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asked about the Competent Authority – what qualities are expected and to what extent the Minister will seek its counsel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Competent Authority will be a civil servant appointed to administer the parts of the Act relating to disclosure requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be made up of officers from MHA, and they will act in accordance with the general directions of the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Alex Yam asked whether it would be an offence if a religious leader made public statements against a law enacted by the Government which runs counter to the beliefs of the religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I presume he means whether such conduct would be grounds for an RO to be issued.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on what the religious leader says, how he says it and to whom he says it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not want to constrain public debate on social issues, even when done on religious grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if a religious group says, you can only vote for people who are of the same religion as you, that is not acceptable and crosses the line.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asks for assurances that the RO will not be used to target any religious community and Mr Alex Yam	asked about the safeguards if the Government becomes “aggressively atheistic” and applies	the MRHA beyond what it was drafted for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The RO has safeguards, which I had mentioned in my opening speech and I will reiterate them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The President decides whether to confirm, vary or cancel the RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PCRH is made up of community leaders – both religious leaders and lay persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All the major religions are represented on the Council.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have powers to call any person to provide information while making their recommendations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have these pieces of legislation and I have made this philosophical point elsewhere: it is a balance of power between the Executive and the individuals and other institutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It shaped values and norms in our society, and very different from every other place around us and further beyond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Alex Yam also asked about recourse for individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a person or religious group is aggrieved by the RO that is issued, they can make representations to the PCRH.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These processes have been put in place to ensure that the Minister’s decision can be reviewed and the RO issued, if appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many Members have spoken in support of the amendment to remove the 14-day notice period in this age of the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if most of the situations will involve the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The RO is meant to be pre-emptive, and to prevent further harm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With the Internet and smartphones, I do not think you can talk about this is brick-and-mortar and this is the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It moves from one to the other very quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A speech to a small group of followers in a room can be recorded and transmitted in a matter of seconds and, from there, it can go viral very quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think a 14-day notice period would be quite ineffective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Anthea Ong said the removal of the 14-day notice period may mean that the Government no longer consults religious groups or stakeholders before the issuance of the RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As my colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling has said, the Government’s preference has always been for the community to resolve the issues of religious disharmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We work closely with religious groups, there are open channels, and this close, consultative relationship has been mentioned by Members, such as Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will continue, even as we determine the action to be taken in each case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the person subject to the RO obviously can exercise his rights to have a review by the PCRH and, ultimately, the decision is to be confirmed or otherwise by the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Alex Yam asked about how the RO would interact with POFMA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: POFMA can be used to direct online platforms, amongst other things, to amplify the corrections to a falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some instances, of course, it can both be false and also come under MRHA, and then, one has got to decide how to deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked why the PCRH can recommend varying a new RO but can only confirm or cancel a proposed direction to extend an existing RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I congratulate him for having read the Bill so closely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the same arrangement for the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister may only direct the extension of an existing RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He cannot change the terms of an existing RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, he either extends it or lets it lapse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All the terms of the RO remain the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hence, similarly, PCRH can only confirm or cancel the RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Douglas Foo had questions on the thresholds for offences in MRHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Douglas Foo asked if the Ministry can provide guidelines on what constitutes offensive statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim asked how we define “wounding” of religious feelings and was concerned that it would cover genuine differences of opinions and views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He cautioned that laws must not end up silencing all discussion of religious topics through ambiguous definitions of illegal behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also asked if proselytisation would be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were adapted from existing offences in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Statements that denigrate another religion will, of course, cross the line.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had the Penal Code for eons and we have had the MRHA for 27 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These terms are not new, and I do not think that anyone complains that there has not been a possibility of discussing viewpoints or that all discussion on religious topics have been silenced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think people understand the norms and values, and there are fairly open discussions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a debate on religious differences gets into a denigration of another religion, insults, incites violence, we will, of course, take action and we have done so in the past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts will take reference from case law to assess the facts of the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But nobody has felt that these laws prevented them from saying what they wanted because most people are sensible and we have created a framework within Singapore for a sensible, practical, wise way of discussing these.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prof Yaacob Ibrahim asked if MRHA offences will apply to intra-faith matters, where persons seek to insult or wound persons of a different denomination of the same religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill defines religious belief or activity to mean holding a religious belief or view or engaging in religious activity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The religious practice or view of a denomination can be distinct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked us to have regard to protecting social harmony, especially in cases where religious leaders stigmatise persons who do not have the same values and exhorts the Government to change policy on religious grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The intent again, I reiterate, is not to stifle conversation about policy issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The role of the law and the Government is to set some boundaries on how these discussions are carried out so that the conversation can be constructive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But apart from the legal framework, the Government seeks to build constructive relationships with stakeholders involved in the debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we do need the law to give that framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the scope of “religious leaders”.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But whether someone is, in fact, a religious leader has got to be a finding of fact based on the assessment of each case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Ms Rahayu Mahzam were concerned about the distinction we have drawn between private and public speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the alleged offender can prove that he made the communication in situations where the parties to the conversation intended it to be heard or seen by themselves, this will be a defence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not want to intrude too much.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They say it to their family members or they say it to their friends in a specific context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not want to necessarily criminalise all of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the burden is on the alleged offender to prove that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked about a person who secretly videotapes the speech and communicates it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a person does this so that action can be taken against the offensive speech in the video, then he is likely to have a defence provided in the Bill as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second element narrows the first to cover circumstances, such as conversations with immediate family, and you will see other examples in the explanatory statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The religious leader will have to show that his conduct falls within this narrower scope.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rationale for the defence is to recognise that there will be situations where the religious leader will want to speak unencumbered and can speak unencumbered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We balanced this with the potential for harm that a speech of a religious leader can cause.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is why the defence for religious leaders is scoped tighter than for persons who are not religious leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam said there could be situations where members of a religious group have repeated private discussions with different groups of people to preach hatred and disharmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Anthea Ong suggested the inclusion of “Stephen’s Code” in MRHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Her suggestion may not deal with the outcome of the person's speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is an important aspect that we have to take into account in determining whether the law should step in for conduct of speech that is motivated by religious prejudice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our approach is for persons who are not religious leaders, their conduct must have an additional element of being likely to disturb public peace.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also provided a defence for a person who is pointing out in good faith conduct which could constitute an offence under section 17F, for the purposes of removal of such material.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the rehabilitation of offenders that commit criminal offences under MRHA, like inciting hatred.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a good suggestion and we will look into it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about whether we would have oversight of foreign guest speakers who come here without a permit, especially in situations where they approach individual places of worship and speak with smaller groups of people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Joan Pereira had a related question on how we can facilitate whistleblowing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are existing requirements that local organisations which bring in foreign preachers to speak in Singapore must comply with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to apply for the appropriate permits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are penalties under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the Minister’s powers to create offences in the MRHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These powers will be used to create regulatory offences to facilitate disclosure requirements introduced through the MRHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how we can conduct online checks on materials and use technology to stop comments or posts which may incite religious disharmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to take a balanced and pragmatic approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, we restrict access to content that is against public interest when it comes to our attention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also asked about how the ROs can be enforced against online service providers and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about how action can be taken for posts on influential pages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We mitigate the deleterious effects of harmful online content in other ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For social media platforms like Facebook or Twitter, IMDA can issue a takedown notice to remove offensive posts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I move now on to the Community Remedial Initiative (CRI).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim has said that while there is a need for strong and decisive measures for serious cases, there are other times where engagement and dialogue will be more appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Using the weight of the law at first instance is not always the best way to resolve religious disharmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if it would be better to vest the Attorney-General with the power to issue CRI, bringing this closer to a conditional warning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng has also asked whether the CRI can be a sentencing option for the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We wanted to look for a community-based way of dealing with such issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is not appropriate to leave it with the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is especially important in the context of religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should not force people to do what their faith militates against them to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we must leave it voluntary and we leave it as something that you can consider doing and then, later on, in terms of whether further action is taken, this is something that can be taken into account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any improvement of understanding on the part of the offender should be done on a voluntary basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This option would be better than forcing someone through the law to "reform".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will work with the religious leaders and communities to ensure that the actions under the CRI are appropriate and beneficial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Alex Yam asked if we had taken reference from other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we wanted to see how we can deal with these issues in a different, non-legal way, as far as possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke in my opening speech about how the Young Sikh Association reached out to social media influencer, Ms Sheena Phua, and dealt with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Alex Yam brought up this incident as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Joan Pereira said some offenders may go through the motions of the CRI without any sincere intention, to avoid criminal prosecution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Desmond Choo had concerns that the CRI would be taken advantage of.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before the issuance of the CRI, we will assess the circumstances of each case carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, like the young men of the Young Sikh Association, we should take a chance that the CRI will help some people and some communities to mend communal relations without having to involve the law unnecessarily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked if there are plans to use the CRI more widely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will observe how the CRI improves our response to conduct that undermines religious harmony and then learn along the way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One point he made was that, in Singapore, politicians are often seen with religious leaders, and it gives a picture of mixing religion with politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say with wisdom and commonsense and that this is normal in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not live apart from religion; we do not live apart from religious leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you take my Ministry, MHA, it is quite an important part of what we do, interacting closely with religious leaders, constantly being photographed as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, for Government leaders to cut off, not have contact with religious leaders, this will not be wise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Good deep friendships between Government leaders and religious leaders are extremely important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It helps to build trust, bonds and that is important for society as a whole and allows issues to be dealt with in an atmosphere of trust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the key is to do it with wisdom, clarity of position and mutual understanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, in Singapore, we do it publicly, openly and we celebrate that relationship.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the Prime Minister on 15 April 2015 at the Taoist Federation's Silver Jubilee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is important that he is there, standing together with the Archbishop and various other leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the next picture, you see him at the consecration ceremony of a Hindu temple last year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does the Prime Minister say, "No, I don't go for this"?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is the Prime Minister, he represents all of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us move on to the next slide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have entered St Andrew's Cathedral; spoke with 400-plus pastors and we were photographed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Deputy Prime Minister went to a meeting with volunteers from RPG, I think, on 7 September.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a constant thing that we all do and that builds the trust and the bonds between the religious leaders and Government leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is not only Government leaders who do it, as you can see.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can see that it is cross-party, right?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are quite a few pictures of Workers' Party Members with religious leaders and they are across all religions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I thought that was enough to make the point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said it has to be done with mutual understanding and that we are neutral.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I will repeat very strongly: these interactions, the building of bonds, are extremely important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if a political leader is invited – taking the example that Mr Pritam Singh gave – during a period of celebration, say, celebration of the nation, a significant date for the country, say, the 50th Anniversary Celebrations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our tradition in Singapore, as you can see from all of this, we go.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are celebrating a national event and it is important for a Minister to be there to show that all faiths, all sections of the society are celebrating the success of the nation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And does he not go simply because it coincides with the run-up to a general election which one can expect any time?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we have to be sensible enough to say what is the occasion, is it a national event, is the Prime Minister or any other Minister being invited in his capacity as a Minister, or a senior leader in the Government, and what is the message that is being sent?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it a celebration by the religious community of the success of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Shanmugam, would you need another five minutes or so?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think a bit more than five minutes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another point that Mr Pritam Singh made, of religious leaders being seen with political leaders during elections, if the religious leaders are lay religious leaders, they have civil and political rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had Ministers, Members of Parliament who were lay preachers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, they hold senior positions in a religious organisation and who are lay persons who hold other jobs and businesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said, they can be Members of Parliament, they can be Ministers and you cannot be saying they cannot exercise their rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is difficult to draw bright lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I will agree with this point, because we have got to look at these things with care and without a party lens, to decide on what is good for Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must handle these issues with sensibility, care and wisdom.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is not the first time religious leaders and organisations have expressed a view on a piece of legislation or Government policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you will see, December 2010, October 2016 on the casinos and gambling.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the National Council of Churches of Singapore: "We speak against the building of a casino in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Council urges the Government to review this decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The family and social fabric of our nation is currently not strong enough." And if you see, Singapore Islamic Scholars and Religious Teachers Association (PERGAS), October 2016, this is regarding online gambling: "PERGAS would like to voice its concern regarding the Government's approval of online gambling.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Erosion of moral values within the community." I can refer to other examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Members can see that they were quite uncomfortable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government did not tell them "You should not be expressing your views".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that answers Ms Sylvia Lim's questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should we have told them that they are not to comment?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This, again, would suggest not practical to draw very clear bright lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Needs to be dealt with with sensitivity, understanding and some care.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For MRHA, there were substantive consultations with the religious groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Religious leaders in Singapore know they should not be engaging in general political discourse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, again, approaching this without a party lens, the questions are: what is good for Singapore and what is doable?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MRHA, obviously, they will comment and it is understandable that they comment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if they did not support it and made their lack of support public in the way they talked about the casinos and the way they talked about online gambling, it would be no different from how they had reacted earlier on other occasions, if they had said "We do not support this".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think we can completely deny them the right to express some views on some pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, both parties must understand that the language must be one of mutual respect and does not cross over into being partisan and political.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about religious leaders making statements during elections – "vote wisely", "vote for stability" and so on – again, I think the principles ought to be: be careful, be temperate, be wise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I agree that for the good of Singapore, we do not want religious leaders to get into the arena and become partisan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I cannot see that any lines have been crossed so far.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lot of care has to be exercised by the religious leaders if they choose to make statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is in the interest of everyone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member had a couple of technical questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, how the RO is consistent with Article 15 of the Constitution because the RO seeks to constrain some rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Moving on to a query on section 16F that states that an RO has effect despite other written laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is in very, very limited circumstances, but let me give an example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I talked about foreign influence through corporations, companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 145(5) of the Companies Act says there should be at least one director – it is a provision known to all lawyers – who is ordinarily resident in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But supposing we issue an RO because we believe that that company, that person, is subject to foreign inference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, despite section 145(5) of the Companies Act saying that you need at least one person who is resident in Singapore, the RO will take precedence over section 145(5).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, section 16F is to ensure that the religious group cannot refuse to comply with an RO for such reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, he gave a specific illustration and asked whether that would be a breach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, I would like to ask him if that statement is hypothetical or whether it is actual and whether it has actually been made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I will, secondly, tell him that on the specific illustration, the substantive law is broadly similar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at section 17F and compare it with sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code, which I am sure he is very familiar with, you will see that it is broadly, not that different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will depend on what is the intent of the person saying it and the way and purpose for which the statement was made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member made a second point on issues relating to the practice of religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But those comments do not arise from these amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some even in Europe create a lot of obstruction, for example, on the building of mosques and the practice of Islam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, as I said earlier, the Government allocates land for the building of mosques, only for Muslims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That approach is not taken for any other religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For other religions, you got to bid for the land.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is done without tender and makes the access to the practice of Islam easily accessible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have set our case very strongly against Islamophobia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we see any such practice, we will move.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Earlier, a gentleman was sent to prison and caned for writing on a Mass Rapid Transit wall certain derogatory remarks about Muslims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a very serious statement and a statement with serious implications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it contradicts everything that we hold as central and important in Singaporee and it is a fundamental value.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we went out and asked Singaporeans, I think they will be quite shocked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inevitably, if you allow religion to play a significant role in politics, then those who are part of the majority religion must have the biggest say, or plurality, at least, will have the biggest say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you think the position of religious minorities will be better or worse?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He quoted what an Islamic scholar might say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What if a text in another religion is critical of all other religions and it tells its followers that non-believers should be shunned?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you say it is not possible to draw bright lights, that the line will be fuzzy, that is different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, anyway, I see your position and I will leave the Chamber with those statements ringing in my head, that you reject the principle of separation of religion from politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many Members have provided suggestions on how we can resolve disputes arising from different religious beliefs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if MHA could consider having a mediation team to resolve disputes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay suggested forming a group of official and religious mediators.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The religious leaders on the NSC broached the idea of a Commitment to Safeguard Religious Harmony to counter segregationist behaviours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition to the NSC, we have the IRCCs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are in every constituency and they seek to promote racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can be called upon to mediate in incidents which can impact on social cohesion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For private family disputes, such as those highlighted by Ms Irene Quay, the religious leaders work closely with Government agencies to try and find an amicable solution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other than mediation, a number of Members – Prof Yaacob Ibrahim, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Irene Quay, Mr Terence Ho – have talked about the importance of education for members of the public and for our young people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their suggestions also provide a reply to Mr Desmond Choo’s query on how the Government can better bring about awareness among the youths that some discourse is inappropriate in our context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MOE’s curriculum currently inculcates in students values of living harmoniously in our multi-religious context through subjects, such as Character and Citizenship Education and Social Studies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth also has the following programmes to foster better understanding and appreciation of different religions and cultures in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another is Ask Me Anything, Common Senses for Common Spaces and IRCC interfaith dialogues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Different community platforms can help to build and encourage religious harmony in different parts of society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Douglas Foo talked about the tripartite partnership – Government, employers and workers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Irene Quay talked about expanding the membership of the IROs to include more members of different faiths.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Anthea Ong talked about the inclusion of atheists in interfaith dialogues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law sets out the broad parameters of behaviour, but it cannot be the sole driving force to change behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do need the community to come in to ensure that deep and strong bonds are built between and within faiths.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how employers can look out for radicalisation of domestic workers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe the Parliamentary Question reply has dealt with this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says the Courts should act as a safeguard against abuse of powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member will note that section 18 of MRHA is not a total ouster of the Courts’ ability to review decisions or recommendations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court can review decisions and orders under MRHA for some narrow grounds – legality or errors of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He referenced my speech made in the Second Reading of MRHA in 1990.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had a running bet with my people on two things, whether anyone will raise it and no one wanted to take that bet because they expected somebody to raise it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1989, the Government tabled a White Paper setting out the threats to religious harmony and introduced the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill was debated extensively in Parliament and referred to a Select Committee, which made recommendations to improve the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the key recommendations made by the Select Committee was the amendment of the issuance process of the ROs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before the Bill was considered by the Select Committee, it was called the Prohibition Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister was required only to have regard to the recommendations by the PCRH.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He had the sole discretion to decide on the Prohibition Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The President was not involved in the issuance or review of the Order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The current process for the RO has incorporated the recommendations of the Select Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It renamed the Prohibition Order to an RO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in addition to the above, there is a deeper philosophical point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is about what I said just now about the balance of powers among the Executive, other institutions, including the Courts, institutions like the President, the PCRH and, of course, individual members of the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh paid what I think is a compliment by a reference to my speech in 1990, no doubt, so as to make me explain myself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let me say this frankly and completely openly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1990, when I spoke on this, when the MRHA was first put to Parliament, I was a young, common law-trained lawyer with four years of experience and a few months in politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My view was that the legal process was able to resolve all disputes and that was the most suitable approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: About 30 years later, with experience and perspective, I have come to realise that this does not always hold true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is the use of the legal process the best way to deal with all religious issues in society?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How about a firebrand preacher who is unrepentant and not remorseful?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By going to the Courts, you may be able to deal with the preacher.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what of communal relations and the underlying sentiments of the community?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The trial process can often deepen the fault lines and encourage others to do the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can even be counterproductive; the alleged offenders become martyrs for their communities, inflaming tensions even more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will give Members a couple of examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You look at the Bali bomb attacks in October 2002.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The mastermind was put on trial, said the Court verdict was not in line with Islamic teachings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He used his trial repeatedly to condemn the United States (US), its President, Israel, calling them the world’s terrorists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He promised to write a book on jihad.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was the bodyguard of Mr Salman Taseer, a politician with relatively liberal viewpoints in Pakistan and an outspoken critic of the blasphemy laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mumtaz Qadri murdered Salman Taseer, the person he was to protect, claiming it was his religious duty to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Qadri was hailed as a hero by some Islamist groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thousands of activists turned up during the trial to show their support during the trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supporters in 2011 threw rose petals on the armoured vehicle carrying Qadri away from the court, all beamed throughout the world and all over Pakistan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When he was executed, crowds took to the streets to protest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1989, I was quite innocent of these ways of the world – how people actually behave, how they can abuse the legal process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I believe today what I believed in 1989, then I would not be standing here tabling this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I took an active role in conceptualising and working through this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe it to be right for our country and that belief has much to do with what has happened in the last 27 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The formulators of the original MRHA had greater experience, knowledge and foresight than I had.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I spoke, I recall that the current Prime Minister responded to me though he did not refer to me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But after that, in my all youthful innocence, I was not convinced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in the nearly 30 years since MRHA was enacted, we look around us – Al-Qaeda, ISIS, communal violence in Myanmar, Sri Lanka and more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are disputes between all major religions across the world, and abuse of major religions by politicians and religious leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Through this, we stand proud, a beacon of religious tolerance and social harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My opening speech sets out the principles we have applied, the policies we have put in place and how they have all worked together to help keep religious harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The MRHA tries to balance different methods of resolving disputes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The RO is pre-emptive, to stop the spread of speech or material that can cause widespread harm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is also used to curb malicious foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We use this in situations where the person and the offended community are willing to meet to mend relations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prosecution is used in serious cases, where the person incites violence or his conduct poses a threat to the public peace and order of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In such cases, criminal sanctions are appropriate to deter others from similar conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It also provides for severe punishments to reflect the person's culpability and conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had some incidents of religious disharmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nine years ago, we had a Christian pastor Rony Tan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He made offensive remarks against Buddhism and Taoism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These video clips were available on his church's website.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We spoke with him, he apologised publicly to the religious leaders of the affected communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because norms have been shaped and values have been shaped.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does that mean we do not practise our religions?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many religious people in this House and outside.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the Institute of Policy Studies survey shows that Singaporeans are very deeply religious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that does not prevent us from having harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We try, as best as we can, to deal with the issues with wisdom and commonsense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some people say, "This Government has done so; how do we trust future governments?" I think that is the constant paradox about Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires good governance for the country to succeed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way each of the situations was dealt with – wisdom, commonsense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a core value of our country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And fundamentally, our people trust the Government to keep to this and to apply the rules fairly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The MRHA comes in, gives powers to the Government to step in where necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are religiously diverse, yet live in harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The most powerful point, as I have said earlier about the MRHA, we have never had to use it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once in a while, we have to go and talk to some religious leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But our public approach, setting the norms, our speeches, policies, holding the ring neutrally, fair approach, constant positive engagement with religious groups and swift action taken, together with the MRHA and other laws, have created the current situation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of these and more have meant that we have managed to create a framework of positive norms and values for our society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Basically, I just want to touch on two points.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The first one would be, the Minister mentioned that, in my speech, I mentioned that I disagree.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Maybe, I would like to reiterate my speech in Malay and I would actually translate to English.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: And I actually continued by saying that I understand that Christianity also believes the same, of which religion cannot be separated from politics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, I am not so sure the Minister mentioned that he counter-checked with that particular someone on that particular sentence of mine, whether he checked with the same person, the content, in the context of what I have spoken about for this point, rather than just one particular sentence and the Minister tends to choose to amplify by saying that I totally disagree with this principle.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I did not say that I quote from a preacher who says those who believe Jesus as the Son of God will end up in hell fire.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I mentioned that it is a quote from the Quran.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, you are seeking a clarification from the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I understood the second one has been a quote that the Member is making and I gave my points, just to clarify on that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are other religious texts which also, if read out of context – I am not saying you are reading the Quran out of context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not want to discuss or debate Quran.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But other religious texts that if you read them out of context, a literal reading could suggest that non-believers should be dealt with harshly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we need to be careful in Singapore how these things are preached and brought about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe that, for example, in Singapore, when people refer to the Old Testament, they would do it with context and sensitivity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is what the Christian preachers tell me, that they will do it with sensitivity and they will take a lot of care.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because, by referencing to other religions, if everybody starts saying we do not accept the separation of religion and politics in Singapore, do you accept that there will be severe consequences?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is why, in this country, we have always brought the religions together.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have also said there has got to be a separation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, perhaps, just to be clear, does the Member accept the principle or does he not accept the principle?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I think the Minister needs to look in what context I am saying this principle which I may not fully agree.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: As I mentioned, I would like to highlight that —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Manap, the Minister is asking you a question.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I do not think you need to read from —

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: If he just picked on that particular sentence, it will be out of context.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I do not think it is accurate and, in a way, fair for me.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Can you not read the whole thing again, because we have heard it already?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I said that as a Muslim, we learn Islam and we accept Islam as a way of life.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, I am not so sure what is the issue with me saying that, in the context of me as a Muslim which, in a way, cannot fully agree, in terms of the principle of the separation of religion and politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Maybe, please explain, Mr Manap, what do you mean by religion and politics here?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, every aspect of life would include politics, right?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You just said every aspect of life must be covered by religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if a religious leader or Muslim religious leader comes out and says, "Islam covers all aspects of life and, therefore, Muslims must vote for Muslims".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suppose that follows, does not it, based on your position?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I did mention in my speech that we should not use religion for the benefit of politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if someone were to say religion cannot be separated from politics and it covers all aspects of life, and therefore it should impact on Government's policy formulation as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must follow from what you say; that this comes through, surely.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, especially in these policies, there is the element of being intertwined between politics and religion, which cannot be separated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Manap, in this clarification and discussion, I do not think that we are going anywhere because we are going around in circles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Either your words mean something – (a) or (b).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you believe, I ask you for the final time, religion and politics should be kept separate?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am just asking you: do you believe that religion should be kept separate from politics?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I am asking you, would you be prepared to answer honestly?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you believe religion should be kept separate from politics?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I do not wish to be engaged in such a debate because as I mentioned just now, it is clearly stated in my speech.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe that your clarification, Minister, is directed to my speech.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: And I have clearly mentioned in my speech my stand as a Muslim which I see: Islam is a way of life; in the process, in every aspect of life, including politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Manap, I am entitled to ask you, based on that, a further clarification: do you believe that religion should be kept separate from politics in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister, I think Mr Pritam Singh wants to raise something.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Perhaps Mr Manap can be given a final opportunity to answer the question I just asked.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think Mr Manap has answered the question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, Mr Deputy Speaker, I was attempting to intervene to just make clear what the position has to be in Singapore, as a minority Member of Parliament for any party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You represent not just members of your own community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the only way to move forward is to accept that there has to be a certain degree of understanding towards other faiths and move forward in a way which accepts that we must be mindful of introducing religion into politics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think where Mr Manap is coming from is faith.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And in his faith, it is a value system; I believe the Christian faith is similar.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But, ultimately, for a Member of Parliament of any political party in Singapore, I think it is important that you remember that you have to represent the interest of every community, not just yours.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, I assume you are speaking for yourself because you should not be speaking for Mr Manap.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, I would like to thank the Minister for answering the questions which I posed which I find quite helpful.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And I think I should also clarify why I asked the question about Article 15.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Of course, I did not overlook Article 15(4) and what it provides and, in a sense, the Minister’s answer was predictable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I felt it was important to put it on record, as a point of reference later on, to make it clear that Parliament did consider this point and it was debated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure that Ms Sylvia Lim is asking me any specific question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we will have to consult the religious groups on the appropriate activities and some of them could include private or public apologies, speaking with the religious leaders of the affected community to better understand their views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the Member also asked about the repercussions of genuine oversights for disclosure of donations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of them may also not have, as the Member said, adequate resources to dedicate for such disclosures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we will work with the religious groups on the implementation of these requirements and will give them short-term exemptions where required.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member also asked whether there is going to be a help desk or resource centre to educate and assist religious groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The CA which will be set up, we will work with the religious groups to see how we can assist, but we are also limited in our manpower.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is something that has to be dealt with, with some element of commonsense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member asked about foreign donations received by non-registered local religious groups which are affiliated with international religious organisations.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: If I may ask, the fifth one was: we are witnessing a rise of many charismatic and fanatic preachers who have built massive followers in tens of millions online, they are passing divisive values and teachings.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: How can we safeguard Singaporeans from having access to such contents on social platforms, given the introduction of the extraterritorial clause in this amendment Bill?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are putting the extraterritorial clause, but I think the Members would recognise it is not easy to go and find these people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not think I want to mislead anyone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will do our best, but that does not mean that we can keep everything out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Deputy Speaker, just one clarification on the point the Minister raised at the end about the position he took in 1990.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Actually, I think it was an eminently sensible position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Of course, I do not have the benefit of 30 years of being in this House, and having been in MHA for many, many years now to take a different position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I do distinctly remember in his speech, the Minister spoke about the concern of that individual in Pakistan, Qadri, who took advantage, basically, of that whole judicial process by bringing more attention to his cause.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister did mention in his speech in 1990 that there is always the prospect of modifying judicial procedures and processes to deal with that sort of a problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was just one sentence if I remember correctly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think the important point is the separation of powers doctrine, the idea that every man or woman in the country has the opportunity to go before a Court of law to examine what they have been accused of.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is not a new exception we are making.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are keeping to the exception that was made, but even since my speech in 1990, a further structure was set up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The structure was not a judicial process per se, but a separate independent review process, going up all the way to the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sorry, by the way, Qadri is much more recent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think it had taken place in 1990.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: And if so, what would be an ideal standard of care, especially in cases where the characterisation might be offensive or hurtful?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am the Minister for Home Affairs, Minister for Law, and I can tell Members what the law is and what should not be done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond that, I think those are matters where we certainly can talk to the religious leaders in a private setting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I do not think I should be commenting publicly on how I want religious leaders to behave and what standards they ought to meet.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: At the beginning of my speech, I asked about the new provisions – I think the provision is section 17E(1) and (2) – and I cited the example of 2016 when a Singaporean man threatened to open fire on a Facebook comment, and the Facebook community is a religiously based one.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: So, now that we have these new provisions, would something like this come under that as an offence under the new provisions?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know enough of those facts to be able to tell the Member whether he could have been charged here.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Irshad, do you have a new clarification?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We should not be in debate; this is clarification time.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: I do not have a new clarification, but I am very troubled by what was shared in the conversation between Minister Shanmugam and Member of Parliament Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: You can seek a clarification of the Minister’s speech, but you are not in a position to make a personal statement unless it relates to yourself.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Perhaps I would like to put it across as a clarification for the Minister and then I will ask a question and propose the point.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: From what I understand from Member of Parliament Faisal Manap's —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ask the Minister for clarification on his speech.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Minister, you mentioned very clearly you wanted a clarification from the Member of Parliament that religion has to be separate from politics.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: However, what I felt is that I think it has to be explicitly mentioned and to be made clear that, as a Muslim, you can have any personal view and opinion whether you believe that religion is also encompassing as part of your faith and your lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: But as a nation, I think we have to understand that we have to have a secular country.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: As a secular nation, we cannot impose our religious values on the common spaces of everybody.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has never been said to me in the terms that Mr Manap put it today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Everyone would say their personal views will be, can be, influenced by religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many in Cabinet, many Members of Parliament are deeply religious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when you make your decisions, you cannot put aside your religious self but you must take into account everybody else and you act neutrally; and you take the position for the benefit of all Singaporeans, even if you believe that that may not be consistent with your religious beliefs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we meet with the Muslim leaders, when we meet with the Muslim clerics, when we meet with the Mufti, then we meet with the Christian leaders, they understand that, they accept it and they say that is the only way in which we can proceed with governing Singapore and living in Singapore, not just for us as a Government but for them as religious leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Manap has introduced a new element in that process today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that is something for him, and others around him, to think about.
